Generalised-Edged Quivers and Global Forms
Julius F. Grimminger, William Harding, and Noppadol Mekareeya

Abstract
Non-simply laced quivers, despite the lack of complete Lagrangian descriptions, play an important role in characterising moduli spaces of supersymmetric field theories. Notably, the moduli space of instantons in non-simply laced gauge groups can be understood by means of such quivers. We generalise the notion of non-simply laced unitary quivers to those whose edges carry two labels ( p , q ) (p,q) , dubbed ( p , q ) (p,q) -edged quivers. The special case of ( p , 1 ) (p,1) corresponds to a conventional non-simply laced edge studied in the literature. In the case of unframed ( p , q ) (p,q) -edged quivers, we show how to parametrise the lattice of magnetic fluxes upon ungauging the decoupled U ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathrm{U}(1) , and how one can pick sublattices thereof corresponding to different global forms of the quiver related by discrete gauging. This form of discrete gauging can be applied to any unframed unitary quivers, not just ones with generalised edges. We utilise both the Hilbert series and the superconformal index to study moduli spaces and ’t Hooft anomalies. In particular, we study mixed ’t Hooft anomalies between a one-form symmetry and a zero-form continuous topological symmetry in various ( p , q ) (p,q) -edged quivers. We also provide an alternative realisation of the moduli space of 𝔰 ​ 𝔬 ​ ( 2 ​ n + 1 ) \mathfrak{so}(2n+1) instantons via gauging discrete symmetries in supersymmetric QCD with a symplectic gauge group and a large number of flavours.

Introduction and Summary

Three dimensional
\mathcal{N}=4
quiver gauge theories and their moduli spaces play a prominent role in the study of superconformal field theories (SCFTs) with 8 supercharges in various spacetime dimensions. Various properties of such SCFTs may not be accessible through the weakly coupled Lagrangian description. Nevertheless, the Higgs branch at the strongly coupled point of a number of such theories can be expressed via the Coulomb branch of certain 3d
{\cal N}=4
quiver theories, known as
magnetic quivers
, many of which can be obtained from a brane system; see e.g.
[
1
,
2
]
.

Conventional
{\cal N}=4
quivers with simply laced edges and unitary gauge groups naturally appear as worldvolume theories of D3 branes in Hanany-Witten D5-D3-NS5 brane configurations
[
3
]
. Adding an O3 orientifold plane to such a brane system changes the gauge groups in the quiver from unitary to orthosymplectic; see e.g.
[
4
]
. Adding an ON orientifold plane (
\mathrm{ON}^{-}
or
\widetilde{\mathrm{ON}}^{-}
to be precise) to the brane system produces a unitary non-simply laced quiver
[
5
,
6
]
; see also
[
7
,
8
,
9
]
for a similar type of brane configurations. The non-simply laced edge in the latter is generally not a representation of the accustomed hypermultiplet. In fact, neither a Lagrangian description nor a Higgs branch construction of such quivers is known in general. Nevertheless, the Coulomb branch moduli space can be constructed. In this paper, we generalise the notion of the non-simply laced edge to a more general one, known as a
(p,q)
-edge, carrying a label
(p,q)
. As will be made more precise in the next section, one can think of a non-simply laced edge as that with a label
(p,1)
.

For an unframed
(p,q)
-edged quiver, there is an overall
\U(1)
that acts trivially on the generalised edges. Upon computing the Coulomb branch of such a quiver, one needs to ungauge such an overall
\U(1)
. One of the key points of this paper is to provide a general prescription to do so. A crucial step is to find a parametrisation of the lattice of the gauge magnetic fluxes. We also demonstrate how one can pick sublattices that lead to gauging a
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
zero-form symmetry.
1
1

1

Modifying the magnetic lattice in Coulomb branch computations was considered in the context of non-simply laced quivers in
[
10
]
and in the context of orthosymplectic quivers, and unitary quivers with a single SU node, in
[
11
]
.
This procedure leaves the Higgs branch invariant, but acts as a quotient on the Coulomb branch, as well as produces a dual
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
one-form symmetry. We study different global forms of the unframed
(p,q)
-edged quiver that are related to each other by such discrete gaugings. A key tool we employ is the Coulomb branch Hilbert series, computed via the monopole formula
[
12
]
, which was generalised in
[
6
]
to allow for non-simply laced quivers. In this paper, we generalise the latter even further to deal with the
(p,q)
-edged quivers. Whenever the theory in question admits a Lagrangian description, we examine it using the superconformal index
[
13
,
14
,
15
,
16
,
17
,
18
,
19
,
20
]
.

We finally remark that non-simply laced quivers have appeared as magnetic quivers not only for brane systems involving orientifold planes, but also to describe certain phases in brane systems with identical branes of self-intersection zero
[
21
,
22
]
. A natural question is to realise general
(p,q)
-edged quivers from the brane perspective. We leave this problem for future work.

Organisation of the paper.

In Section
2
, we give a detailed introduction to unitary quivers with generalised
(p,q)
-edges and their Coulomb branches for various choices of global forms. We compare this in some examples with
wreathed quivers
, which were first explored in
[
23
]
and were recently studied in
[
24
,
25
]
. In Section
3
, we present additional examples, including an Abelian theory, in which the quiver has a Lagrangian description and we can study it using the superconformal index, and a non-Abelian theory. We also examine mixed ’t Hooft anomalies between a one-form symmetry and a zero-form continuous topological symmetry in various
(p,q)
-edged quivers. In Section
4
, we demonstrate how to realise the moduli space of
\mathfrak{so}(2n+1)
instantons via gauging discrete symmetries in supersymmetric QCD with a symplectic gauge group and a large number of flavours. In Appendix
A
, we illustrate in many examples how to parametrise the magnetic lattice. Finally, in Appendix
B
, we present a way to produce quivers which are quotients of the form
\mathbb{H}^{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}
, where the
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
can act with various charges on the different coordinates.

2
Coulomb Branch of Unitary Quivers with
(p,q)
-Edges

Coulomb branches of 3d
{\cal N}=4
(simply laced) unitary quivers are well studied in the literature. These quivers consist of a collection of gauge nodes (depicted by circles), flavour nodes (depicted by boxes), and (possibly multiple) edges between such nodes. If there are no flavour nodes in the quiver, it is called
unframed
; if there are flavour nodes in the quiver, it is called
framed
.

In this section we introduce unitary quivers with
(p,q)
-edges, which are generalisations of the non-simply laced quivers first introduced in
[
6
]
. Coulomb branches of non-simply laced unitary quivers have also been extensively studied in the literature, and the generalisation to
(p,q)
-edged quivers is natural. However, in the following, we make some necessary clarifications on how to deal with unframed non-simply laced unitary quivers (and, more generally,
(p,q)
-edged ones). In particular, we address how to decouple the freely acting U
(1)
gauge group, and how this leads to a notion of
global form
of an unframed unitary quiver.

2.1
(p,q)
-Edged Unitary Quivers

In a simply laced unitary quiver, an edge between two gauge nodes U
(v_{1})
and U
(v_{2})
represents a hypermultiplet in the bifundamental representation
(\mathbf{v_{1}},\overline{\mathbf{v_{2}}})
2
2

2

The hypermultiplet is made of two chiral multiplets in the representation
(\mathbf{v_{1}},\overline{\mathbf{v_{2}}})\oplus(\overline{\mathbf{v_{1}}},\mathbf{v_{2}})
.
of U
(v_{1})\times
U
(v_{2})
:

(2.1)

The contribution of this hypermultiplet to the conformal dimension of a monopole operator of magnetic charge
(m_{1,a_{1}},m_{2,a_{2}})
, with
a_{1}=1,\dots,v_{1}
and
a_{2}=1,\dots,v_{2}
, is

2\Delta_{\mathrm{hyper}_{\eqref{eq:hyper1}}}(m_{1,a_{1}},m_{2,a_{2}})=\sum_{a_{1}=1}^{v_{1}}\sum_{a_{2}=1}^{v_{2}}|m_{1,a_{1}}-m_{2,a_{2}}|~.

2\Delta_{\mathrm{hyper}_{\eqref{eq:hyper2}}}(m_{1},m_{2})=|p\,m_{1}-q\,m_{2}|\;.

(2.4)

One can ask for a generalisation of the
(p,q)
-edge in the case where
v_{1},v_{2}>1
. A natural generalisation would be to consider the representation
(\mathrm{Sym}^{p}\mathbf{v_{1}},\mathrm{Sym}^{q}\overline{\mathbf{v_{2}}})
. This is of course a perfectly nice representation for a hypermultiplet to be in. We can take for example
v_{1}=2
,
v_{2}=1
,
p=2
, and
q=1
. The contribution of this hypermultiplet to the conformal dimension of a monopole operator of magnetic charge
(m_{1,1},m_{1,2},m_{2})
is

\begin{split}&2\Delta_{\mathrm{hyper}_{(\mathrm{Sym}^{2}\mathbf{2},\overline{\mathbf{1}})}}(m_{1,1},m_{1,2},m_{2})\\
&=|2\,m_{1,1}-m_{2}|+|2\,m_{1,2}-m_{2}|+|(m_{1,1}+m_{1,2})-m_{2}|\;.\end{split}

(2.5)

However, this is not what we have in mind. A notion of non-simply laced edge, that is a
(p,1)
-edge in our language, was introduced in
[
6
]
(based on Hanany-Witten type brane systems with orientifolds, and 3d mirror symmetry). For a
(2,1)
-edge between a rank
v_{1}=2
and a rank
v_{2}=1
node, the hypermultiplet contribution to the conformal dimension of a monopole operator of magnetic charge
(m_{1,1},m_{1,2},m_{2})
, is

2\Delta_{(2,1)\mathrm{-edge}}(m_{1,1},m_{1,2},m_{2})=|2\,m_{1,1}-m_{2}|+|2\,m_{1,2}-m_{2}|\;,

(2.6)

which is different of course from (
2.5
). The edge does not represent a hypermultiplet in a representation of U
(v_{1})\times
U
(v_{2})
! The theory denoted by a quiver involving such edges is hence non-Lagrangian, and yet remains to be fully understood. Such quivers do however lead to a well defined notion of Coulomb branch
[
6
,
26
]
.

For generic
v_{1}
and
v_{2}
, we propose a
(p,q)
-edge

.

2.1.1
Notation

Thus far, generic
(p,q)
-edges have not been studied in the literature,
4
4

4

With the exception of
[
26
]
.
and hence no notation has been introduced. We will denote
N

(p,q)
-edges between a rank
v_{1}
and a rank
v_{2}
gauge node as

v_{1}
v_{2}
p
q
N

(2.9)

(2.15)

2.1.2
Unframed Unitary Quivers and their Adjacency Matrix

In the following, we consider unframed unitary quivers with generalised edges.
Let
i,j
, with
i\geq j
, label two nodes in the quiver. Then, we define
e_{ij}
to be the number of generalised edges from node
i
to node
j
, and we denote by
(p_{k},q_{k})_{k=1,\dots,e_{ij}}
the charges of these generalised edges. We require that

\begin{split}&\text{$\frac{p_{1}}{q_{1}}=\dots=\frac{p_{e_{ij}}}{q_{e_{ij}}}$~,~ and}\\
&\text{if $i=j$~,~ $\frac{p_{1}}{q_{1}}=\dots=\frac{p_{e_{ii}}}{q_{e_{ii}}}=1$~.}\end{split}

(2.16)

These are not necessary conditions for the underlying quiver to make sense. For example, if the ranks of all gauge nodes are one, then any hypermultiplets can have arbitrary charges under all gauge groups, and this still gives a perfectly well-defined Lagrangian. However, these conditions seem to be obeyed by any quivers (electric or magnetic) which are read from brane systems. It also provides a convenient way to define a notation of the adjacency matrix (see below), which can be interpreted as a generalised Cartan matrix, for a quiver.
5
5

5

We illustrate the significance of conditions (
2.16
) via an example as follows. Let us take a quiver with two
\U(1)
gauge nodes connected by a
(p_{1},q_{1})=(2,1)
-edge and a
(p_{2},q_{2})=(1,3)
-edge so that the conditions (
2.16
) are violated. Let
m_{1}
and
m_{2}
be the gauge fluxes of each gauge node. Then, the conformal dimension of the monopole operator with flux
m_{1}
and
m_{2}
is given by
2\Delta(m_{1},m_{2})=|2m_{1}-m_{2}|+|m_{1}-3m_{2}|
. The adjacency matrix defined in (
2.17
) for this quiver is
A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&3\\
4&-2\end{pmatrix}
. We see that
2\Delta
cannot be written in the form of (
2.32
), namely
|A_{12}m_{1}-A_{21}m_{2}|
.

We define the
adjacency matrix

A
of the quiver by setting

\begin{split}\begin{split}A_{ji}=&\sum_{k=1}^{e_{ij}}q_{k}~,\quad A_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{e_{ij}}p_{k}~\quad\text{for $i>j$}~,\\
A_{ii}=&-2+2\sum_{k=1}^{e_{ii}}p_{k}~\quad\text{for $i=j$}~.\end{split}\end{split}

(2.17)

We refer to a collection of the ranks of the gauge nodes in the quiver as
rank vector
:

\left(v_{i}\right)_{i=1,\dots,n}\;.

(2.18)

The adjacency matrix, together with the rank vector, defines a Coulomb branch, as we will see shortly.

Some examples for quivers, with their corresponding adjacency matrices and rank vectors, are given in the table below.

\lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}&\begin{pmatrix}-2&ap\\
aq&-2\end{pmatrix}&\begin{pmatrix}v_{1}\\
v_{2}\end{pmatrix}\\
\hline\cr\end{array}\end{split}

(2.19)

Note that the map from quiver to adjacency matrix is not one-to-one! The first three quivers in (
2.19
), for example, are distinct, yet they have the same adjacency matrix. This is because the adjacency matrix only captures the information about the singular Coulomb branch.
Hence, one can usually assign many different quivers to a given adjacency matrix. While these quivers have the same singular Coulomb branch, they have different Higgs branches,
6
6

6

It is still not known how to compute the Higgs branch of a generic non-simply laced or
(p,q)
-edged quiver. In a few cases it is possible to obtain the Higgs branch of a non-simply laced quiver via 3d mirror symmetry. Furthermore, it is always possible to directly compute the Higgs branch of a
(p,q)
-edged quiver with Abelian nodes. In this paper, we simply assume the existence of a Higgs branch, and we rarely discuss it.
and they allow for different sets of mass parameters deforming the Coulomb branch.

(2.20)

Such quivers possess the same Coulomb branch:

\mathrm{CB}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{1}\right)=\mathrm{CB}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{2}\right)=\mathrm{CB}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{3}\right)=\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{N}\;.

(2.21)

Yet, the Higgs branches are different:

\begin{split}\mathrm{HB}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{1}\right)&=\overline{\mathrm{min.}A_{N-1}}\;,\\
\mathrm{HB}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{2}\right)&=\mathrm{point}\;,\\
\mathrm{HB}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{3}\right)&=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{C}^{3}|xy=z^{\frac{N}{\mathrm{gcd}(N,N-M)}}\}\;.\end{split}

(2.22)

For
\mathsf{Q}_{1}
, there are
N-1
mass parameters, which allow to completely resolve the Coulomb branch
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{N}
singularity. For
\mathsf{Q}_{2}
, there are no mass parameters, and the Coulomb branch cannot be resolved. For
\mathsf{Q}_{3}
, there is one mass parameter. Turning it on produces a Coulomb branch with two singular points: one of them is locally
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{N-M}
, and the other one is locally
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{M}
.

2.1.3
Symmetrisability and Shortness

We furthermore require
A
to be
symmetrisable
, i.e. there is a shortness vector

\left(s_{i}\right)_{i=1,\dots,n}\;,

(2.23)

such that the following conditions are satisfied:

\begin{split}A_{ij}s_{i}=A_{ji}s_{j}\quad&\forall\,\,i,j=1,\dots,n~\\
\mathrm{gcd}(s_{i})&=1\;.\end{split}

(2.24)

This implies that the quiver can be
unfolded
, i.e. there is a simply laced quiver
\widetilde{\mathsf{Q}}
such that, folding it, gives the non-simply laced quiver
\mathsf{Q}
. A node of shortness
s_{i}
will appear
s_{i}
times in the unfolded quiver.

(2.28)

the corresponding adjacency matrix is non-symmetrisable

A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1&1\\
1&-2&1\\
3&2&-2\end{pmatrix}\;,

(2.29)

meaning that (
2.28
) cannot be unfolded.

2.1.4
Naive Gauge Group and Magnetic Lattice

We refer to the gauge group that is manifest in the quiver diagram, namely

\widetilde{G}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\U(v_{i})~,

(2.30)

as the
naive gauge group
, with magnetic (i.e. coweight) lattice
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
parametrised by magnetic weights
m_{i,a_{i}}
, with
a_{i}=1,\dots,v_{i}
and
i=1,\dots,n
.
7
7

7

As already anticipated in Footnote
3
, we remark that, when
v_{i}=1
, we suppress the subscript
a_{i}=1
and we simply denote the magnetic weights by
m_{i}
.

Unless stated explicitly, such as around (
2.45
), we generally take the magnetic weights to be integers. We also define

d_{i}=\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}m_{i,a_{i}}

(2.31)

as the charge of the topological symmetry associated with the gauge group
\U(v_{i})
.

2.1.5
Conformal Dimension and Shift Symmetry

The conformal dimension of a bare monopole operator is given by

2\Delta(\bm{m})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}\sum_{b_{j}=1}^{v_{j}}\mathrm{sign}(A_{ij})\left|A_{ij}m_{i,a_{i}}-A_{ji}m_{j,b_{j}}\right|\;.

(2.32)

It has a shift symmetry – corresponding to the U
(1)\subset\widetilde{G}
acting trivially on the edges (i.e. generalised hypermultiplets) – generated by the
shift vector

\delta\in\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}~,\hskip 10.00002pt\text{with}\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{gcd}(\delta_{i,a_{i}})=1\;,

(2.33)

such that

2\Delta(\bm{m}+x\delta)=2\Delta(\bm{m})\;,\hskip 10.00002pt\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}\;.

(2.34)

It is simple to check that

\delta_{i,a_{i}}=s_{i}\;.

(2.35)

We refer to the one-dimensional sublattice generated by the shift vector
\delta
as

\Lambda_{\delta}\subset\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}\;.

(2.36)

2.1.6
Weyl Chamber

Given the Weyl group of
\widetilde{G}

W_{\widetilde{G}}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}S_{v_{i}}~,

(2.37)

then the Weyl chamber of the magnetic lattice of
\widetilde{G}
, namely
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}/W_{\widetilde{G}}
, can be parametrised by setting

-\infty<m_{i,1}\leq m_{i,2}\leq\dots\leq m_{i,v_{i}}<\infty\hskip 10.00002pt\forall\,i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\;.

(2.38)

2.1.7
Ungauging the Decoupled U(1)

Upon decoupling an overall
\U(1)
, we refer to the resulting gauge group as the
true gauge group
:

G=\widetilde{G}/\U(1)\;.

(2.39)

The magnetic lattice of this group is
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}=\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}/\Lambda_{\delta}
, where the Weyl chamber of the magnetic lattice of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
, namely
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}/W_{G}
, can be parametrised via a constraint on the
m_{i,a_{i}}
, while still obeying (
2.38
). There are infinitely many such constraints. In Appendix
A
, many examples of such possible constraints are illustrated very explicitly for several quivers.

For instance, a simple choice for a constraint is

m_{i,a_{i}}\in\{0,\dots,s_{i}-1\}\;,\hskip 10.00002pt\textnormal{for some }i\textnormal{ and }a_{i}\;.

(2.40)

If
s_{i}=1
we can set
m_{i,1}=0
, which is what is commonly done in the literature, and sometimes referred to as “ungauging on the long side” (see e.g.
[
10
]
). Yet, there seems to be a much more general rule.

General rule.

Let us describe a general rule for ungauging an overall
\U(1)
as follows. Let us first choose the following set of non-negative integers:
8
8

8

Throughout this paper, whenever we encounter a
\U(1)
gauge node, i.e.
v_{i}=1
, we suppress the subscript
a_{i}=1
in (
2.41
). Explicitly, for a
\U(1)
gauge node labelled by
i
, we denote the associated non-negative integer in (
2.41
) simply by
\mathfrak{c}_{i}
.

\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}~,\hskip 10.00002pt\text{with}\hskip 10.00002pta_{i}=1,\dots,v_{i}~,\hskip 10.00002pti=1,\dots,n~.

(2.41)

Then, if we define

\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}s_{i}\right)-1\;,

(2.42)

we can pick the following constraint on the magnetic weights:

\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}m_{i,a_{i}}\in\left\{0,1,\dots,\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}\right\}\;,

(2.43)

which can also be generalised to

\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}m_{i,a_{i}}\in\left\{x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}}\right\}\;,\hskip 20.00003pt\textnormal{where}\hskip 20.00003pt(x_{j}\;{\rm mod}\;\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}})=j\;.

(2.44)

Alternative approach.

Let us discuss an alternative, but equivalent, approach in ungauging an overall
\U(1)
. In this method, the magnetic fluxes are allowed to take integral and non-integral values, subject to the condition that each term in the contribution of the matter fields to the conformal dimension is integral. In particular, for a
(p,q)
-edge between the
\U(v_{i})\times\U(v_{j})
gauge group whose contribution is given by (
2.8
), we require that

\begin{split}pm_{i,a_{i}}-qm_{j,a_{j}}\in\mathbb{Z}~\end{split}

(2.45)

and allow
m_{i,a_{i}}
and
m_{j,a_{j}}
to be also non-integral. In the special case in which the gauge groups are Abelian, namely
v_{i}=v_{j}=1
, this theory admits a conventional Lagrangian description in terms of a hypermultiplet of charge
(p,-q)
under
\U(v_{i})\times\U(v_{j})
, and the above condition is simply the Dirac quantisation condition. In the next step, we choose the non-negative integers
\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}
and impose the following constraint on the magnetic fluxes:

\begin{split}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}m_{i,a_{i}}=0~.\end{split}

(2.46)

In contrast to (
2.43
), we restrict the freedom on the linear combination of the left hand side to be zero, but this lack of freedom is compensated by allowing
m_{i,a_{i}}
to take also non-integral values. The two approaches thus yield the same result. In this method, the conditions (
2.45
) and (
2.46
) determine the magnetic lattices that need to be summed over upon computing the Coulomb branch Hilbert series or the superconformal index. This will be demonstrated explicitly via a number of examples in Section
3
.

Let us suppose that the allowed values of the magnetic fluxes are fractional and that, upon writing them in the lowest terms, the largest denominator is
r
. There is a natural
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
zero-form symmetry that acts non-trivially on the monopole operators with such fractional magnetic fluxes. Then, we can turn on a discrete fugacity associated with the
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
symmetry in the Coulomb branch Hilbert series or in the index. This allows for gauging such a symmetry by summing this discrete fugacity over all the
r
-th roots of unity. The gauging leads to a dual
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
one-form symmetry. We finally remark that, upon gauging a discrete one-form symmetry, the magnetic fluxes are also summed over non-integral values. This naturally leads to the dual
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
zero-form as realised above. We will discuss the procedure of gauging one-form symmetries in Section
3.2
.

2.1.8
Good, Ugly, and Bad

Following the nomenclature of
[
27
]
, we call a theory:

•

good, if
2\Delta(\bm{m})>1
for all
\bm{m}\neq 0
;

•

ugly, if
2\Delta(\bm{m})>0
for all
\bm{m}\neq 0
, with some
2\Delta(\bm{m})=1
; and

•

bad, if
2\Delta(\bm{m})\leq 0
for some
\bm{m}\neq 0
.

Good theories have conical Coulomb branches. Ugly theories have Coulomb branches which are a product of a cone and free space. Bad theories have more intricate Coulomb branches. In this paper, we focus mainly on the good and ugly theories.

Balanced nodes.

A useful quantity that can be associated with a node in a quiver is its so-called
balanced
. For a quiver with adjacency matrix
A
and rank vector
v
, the balance of a node
i
, with
A_{ii}=-2
(i.e. no adjoint loops), is given as

b_{i}=\sum_{j}A_{ij}v_{j}\;.

(2.47)

Defining the analogous condition for a balanced node becomes more complex in the presence of adjoint loops. We do not address this case in the present work.

2.1.9
Coulomb Branch Hilbert Series

The Hilbert series of the Coulomb branch of a good or ugly quiver
\mathsf{Q}
can be computed via the monopole formula
[
12
]

\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of $\mathsf{Q}$}\right](t)=\sum_{\bm{m}\in\frac{\Gamma_{G}^{mw}}{W_{G}}}P_{G}(\bm{m},t^{2})t^{2\Delta(\bm{m})}\;,

(2.48)

where

P_{G}(\bm{m},t^{2})=(1-t^{2})\prod_{i=1}^{n}P_{\mathrm{U}(v_{i})}(m_{i},t^{2})\;,

(2.49)

and

P_{\mathrm{U}(v_{i})}\left(m_{i},t^{2}\right)=\prod_{l=1}^{N}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{\lambda_{l}}\frac{1}{\left(1-t^{2k}\right)}\right]

(2.50)

for
\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{N})
a partition of
v_{i}
, which encodes how many
m_{i,a_{i}}
are equal.

This Hilbert series can be refined with respect to the fugacities
w_{i}
associated with the topological symmetries as

\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of $\mathsf{Q}$}\right](t,w_{i})=\sum_{\bm{m}\in\frac{\Gamma_{G}^{mw}}{W_{G}}}P_{G}(m,t^{2})t^{2\Delta(\bm{m})}\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}^{\sum_{a_{i}=1}^{v_{i}}m_{i,a_{i}}}\;,

(2.51)

with the constraint

\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}^{s_{i}v_{i}}=1\;.

(2.52)

If the quiver is bad, then the monopole formula diverges. This is due to the non-conical structure of the Coulomb branch of a bad theory.

2.2
Global Forms

It is by now widely appreciated that, in gauge theory, it is important to specify the precise global form of the gauge group. This choice determines amongst other things the magnetic lattice, and hence affects the Coulomb branch of a
3d

\mathcal{N}=4
gauge theory, while typically leaving the Higgs branch unchanged. For a given
3d

\mathcal{N}=4
gauge theory, the hypermultiplet representations restrict the possible global forms of the gauge group.

Let us take an unframed simply laced unitary quiver with naive gauge group
\widetilde{G}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{U}(v_{i})
, where ungauging the overall U
(1)
is understood, and pick a node labelled by
i_{0}
, with associated gauge node U
(v_{i_{0}})
in the quiver. One way to parametrise the magnetic lattice of the true gauge group, that is
G=\widetilde{G}/\mathrm{U}(1)
, is by setting
d_{i_{0}}=\sum_{a_{i_{0}}=1}^{v_{i_{0}}}m_{i_{0},a_{i_{0}}}\in\{0,\dots,v_{i_{0}}-1\}
:

\begin{split}\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to99.03pt{\vbox to54.06pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 28.65276pt\lower-36.78577pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}}

(2.53)

A different global form of the gauge group compatible with the hypermultiplet representations is

G^{\prime}=\prod_{\underset{i\neq i_{0}}{i=1}}^{n}\mathrm{U}(v_{i})\times\mathrm{SU}(v_{i_{0}})\;,

(2.54)

i.e. we replace U
(v_{i_{0}})
with an SU
(v_{i_{0}})
node, producing a special unitary quiver. The magnetic lattice of

(2.57)

Note that the special cases of
k=v_{i_{0}}
and
k=1
correspond to (
2.55
) and (
2.56
), respectively. Such gauging leads to a dual
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
zero-form symmetry in the resulting theory. We will see via the example below that the presence of the
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
zero-form symmetry is manifest in the periodicity in
d_{i_{0}}
of the Coulomb branch Hilbert series.

We can thus associate many global structures to an unframed unitary quiver in the following way. Pick a node
i_{0}
and impose
d_{i_{0}}\in\{kj|0\leq j\leq(v_{i_{0}}/k)-1\}
for some
k|v_{i_{0}}
.
9
9

9

Note that, once a condition has been imposed on
d_{i_{0}}
of some node labelled by
i_{0}
, one cannot put another condition on
d_{i_{1}}
of some node
i_{1}\neq i_{0}
, as this would reduce the dimension of the magnetic lattice. One could consider picking two distinct nodes,
i_{0}
and
i_{1}
, and impose a condition on a linear combination of
d_{i_{0}}
and
d_{i_{1}}
.
Such a choice has no effect on the Higgs branch of the quiver, yet it does affect the Coulomb branch. In particular, it leads to a
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
quotient of the Coulomb branch of the original theory. This amounts to gauging the
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
zero-form symmetry, which leads to a dual
\mathbb{Z}_{k}
one-form symmetry.

For a general
(p,q)
-edged unframed unitary quiver, with symmetrisable adjacency matrix, the story gets slightly more complicated. We can apply a similar method to that described above by picking a node
i_{0}
and modifying the condition on
d_{i_{0}}
. We observe that, in this case, the order of the discrete zero-form symmetry involves the product
s_{i_{0}}v_{i_{0}}
of shortness
s_{i_{0}}
and the rank
v_{i_{0}}
. Various examples will be provided below and in Section
3
.

Example

Let us consider the following quiver:

3
1
2
2
1
3
3
1
1
1
1
1

(2.58)

with adjacency matrix, rank vector and shortness vector

A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&3&0\\
1&-2&1\\
0&1&-2\end{pmatrix}\,,\;v=\begin{pmatrix}3\\
2\\
1\end{pmatrix}\,,\;s=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
3\\
3\end{pmatrix}\;,

(2.59)

where the true gauge group is

\begin{split}G=\widetilde{G}/\U(1)~,\quad\text{with}\quad\widetilde{G}=\U(3)\times\U(2)\times\U(1)~.\end{split}

(2.60)

Different global structures of this quiver are summarised in Table
1
. Let us discuss them more in detail.

Let us denote by
\bm{m}_{1}=(m_{1,1},m_{1,2},m_{1,3})
,
\bm{m}_{2}=(m_{2,1},m_{2,2})
and
m_{3}
the magnetic fluxes associated with the
\U(3)
,
\U(2)
and
\U(1)
gauge nodes respectively, with

\begin{split}d_{1}=\sum_{1=1}^{3}m_{1,i}~,\quad d_{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{2}m_{2,i}~,\quad d_{3}=m_{3}~.\end{split}

(2.61)

Then, the Coulomb branch Hilbert series of quiver (
2.58
) can be obtained via the monopole formula (
2.51
) as

\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{eq:(3)-{3,1}-(2)-(1)})}\right](t,\bm{w})\\
&=\left(1-t^{2}\right)\sum_{j=0}^{\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}}\sum_{\bm{m}\in\frac{\Gamma_{G}^{mw}}{W_{G}}}P_{\mathrm{U}(3)}(\bm{m}_{1},t^{2})P_{\mathrm{U}(2)}(\bm{m}_{2},t^{2})P_{\mathrm{U}(1)}(m_{3},t^{2})\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\times\left[\prod_{i=1}^{3}w_{i}^{d_{i}}\right]t^{2\Delta(\bm{m})}\delta_{f(\bm{m}),j}~,\end{split}

(2.62)

where we denote by
w_{1}
,
w_{2}
and
w_{3}
the topological fugacities associated with the
\U(3)
,
\U(2)
and
\U(1)
gauge nodes respectively. From (
2.32
), the conformal dimension entering in (
2.62
) reads

\begin{split}2\Delta(\bm{m})=-2&\left(\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq 3}\left|m_{1,i}-m_{1,j}\right|\right)-2\left|m_{2,1}-m_{2,2}\right|\\
+&\left(\sum_{i=1,2,3}\,\sum_{j=1,2}\left|3m_{i,1}-m_{2,j}\right|\right)+\sum_{j=1,2}\left|m_{2,1}-m_{3}\right|~,\end{split}

(2.63)

where we have to take into account the constraint coming from the delta function
\delta_{f(\bm{m}),j}
, which can be explained as follows. The quantity
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}
, defined in (
2.42
), in this case reads

\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathfrak{c}_{1,i}\right)+3\left(\sum_{i=1}^{2}\mathfrak{c}_{2,i}\right)+3\mathfrak{c}_{1}-1~,

(2.64)

moreover we define the function

\begin{split}f(\bm{m})=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathfrak{c}_{1,i}m_{1,i}\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{2}\mathfrak{c}_{2,i}m_{2,i}\right)+\mathfrak{c}_{3}m_{3}\end{split}

(2.65)

implementing (
2.43
), which takes values in
\left\{0,1,\dots,\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}\right\}
for given
\mathfrak{c}_{i,a_{i}}
. Explicitly, some convenient choices to ungauge the decoupled
\U(1)
are the following.

•

We can take
\mathfrak{c}_{1,i}=(1,1,1)
,
\mathfrak{c}_{2,i}=(0,0)
and
\mathfrak{c}_{3}=0
, which is equivalent to
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=2
and
f(\bm{m})=d_{1}
. Then, from the first summation in (
2.62
), we just have to consider the contribution from
d_{1}=\{0,1,2\}
, whereas there is no restriction on
d_{2}
and
d_{3}
. Observe that the resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is periodic in
d_{1}
, with periodicity
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}+1=3
. Explicitly, we can detect such periodicity by looking at the contributions coming from
d_{1}=j=0,\ldots,5
in the first summation in (
2.62
):

\begin{split}{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}j=0~:}\quad&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1+8t^{2}+100t^{4}+645t^{6}+2968t^{8}+10976t^{10}~,}\\
j=1~:\quad&10t^{2}+100t^{4}+640t^{6}+2975t^{8}+10976t^{10}~,\\
j=2~:\quad&10t^{2}+100t^{4}+640t^{6}+2975t^{8}+10976t^{10}~,\\
{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}j=3~:}\quad&{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1+8t^{2}+100t^{4}+645t^{6}+2968t^{8}+10976t^{10}~,}\\
j=4~:\quad&10t^{2}+100t^{4}+640t^{6}+2975t^{8}+10976t^{10}~,\\
j=5~:\quad&10t^{2}+100t^{4}+640t^{6}+2975t^{8}+10976t^{10}~,\end{split}

(2.66)

from which it is clear that every contribution coming from
d_{1}=j=i+3k
, with
i=0,1,2
and
k=0,\ldots,\infty
, is independent of
k
. The periodicity of 3 in
d_{1}
indicates that the theory has a
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
zero-form symmetry. We will gauge this symmetry later.

•

Another possible option is to set
\mathfrak{c}_{1,i}=(0,0,0)
,
\mathfrak{c}_{2,i}=(1,1)
and
\mathfrak{c}_{3}=0
, i.e.
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=5
and
f(\bm{m})=d_{2}
. It follows that, in this case,
d_{2}
takes values in
\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}
, with no restriction on
d_{1}
and
d_{3}
. It follows that the resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is periodic in
d_{2}
, with periodicity
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}+1=6
.

•

Finally, another convenient parametrisation is
\mathfrak{c}_{1,i}=(0,0,0)
,
\mathfrak{c}_{2,i}=(0,0)
and
\mathfrak{c}_{3}=1
, namely
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=2
and
f(\bm{m})=d_{3}
. This choice corresponds to summing over
d_{3}\in\{0,1,2\}
in (
2.62
), with no further restriction on
d_{1}
and
d_{2}
. The resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is periodic in
d_{3}
, with periodicity
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}+1=3
.

In all of such equivalent cases, upon setting the topological fugacities to unity, the Coulomb branch Hilbert series of quiver (
2.58
) admits the following closed form:

\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{eq:(3)-{3,1}-(2)-(1)})}\right](t,w_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1+18t^{2}+65t^{4}+65t^{6}+18t^{8}+t^{10}}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{10}}\\
&=1+28t^{2}+300t^{4}+1925t^{6}+8918t^{8}+32928t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[28t^{2}-106t^{4}+833t^{6}-8400t^{8}+91392t^{10}+\ldots\right]~,\end{split}

(2.67)

where the moment map operators appearing at order
t^{2}
in the series expansion reveal that the Coulomb branch symmetry of the theory is
\mathfrak{so}(8)
. Indeed, the Coulomb branch in question is isomorphic to the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit of
\mathfrak{so}(8)
, denoted by
\overline{\mathrm{min}.D_{4}}

[
28
]

\mathbb{Z}_{2}
quotient.

(2.70)

The resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is

\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{eq:(3)-{3,1}-(2)-(1)})}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}\right](t,w_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1+7t^{2}+101t^{4}+244t^{6}+666t^{8}+650t^{10}+\text{palindrome}+t^{20}}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{10}\left(1+t^{2}\right)^{5}}\\
&=1+12t^{2}+156t^{4}+949t^{6}+4486t^{8}+16416t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[12t^{2}+78t^{4}-351t^{6}-1832t^{8}+23424t^{10}+\ldots\right]~,\end{split}

(2.71)

where the moment map operators appearing at order
t^{2}
in the above series expansion signal that the Coulomb branch symmetry is
\mathfrak{su}(2)^{4}
.

\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient.

We can realise a
\mathbb{Z}_{3}

3
Discrete Gauging and Mixed ’t Hooft Anomalies

In this section, we study zero-form and one-form discrete symmetries in various
(p,q)
-edged quivers and gaugings thereof. We first demonstrate this in an Abelian example, where both the Coulomb branch Hilbert series and the superconformal index are computed. We subsequently examine sequential gauging in a non-Abelian example using the Coulomb branch Hilbert series. We observe that, whenever a non-trivial
(p,q)
-edged quiver possesses a discrete one-form symmetry, possibly arising from gauging the dual zero-form symmetry, the former generally has a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly with some combinations of the continuous topological symmetries in the quiver. This manifests itself in the Hilbert series or in the index, as described in
[
31
]
.

3.1
Abelian Example

Let us consider the following
(p,q)
-edged Abelian quiver

(3.1)

where we denote with
m_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}
, with
i=1,2,3
, the magnetic fluxes associated with the three
\U(1)
gauge nodes. Note that, due to the
\U(1)
gauge groups, this quiver admits a conventional Lagrangian description where the matter fields are the hypermultiplets carrying charges
{(0,1,-2)}
,
{(-1,0,3)}
,
{(2,-3,0)}
under the
\U(1)
gauge groups labelled by
(m_{1},m_{2},m_{3})
respectively.

The adjacency matrix, rank vector and shortness vector associated with (
3.1
) are given respectively by

A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&2&1\\
3&-2&1\\
3&2&-2\end{pmatrix}\,,\;v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
1\\
1\end{pmatrix}\,,\;s=\begin{pmatrix}3\\
2\\
1\end{pmatrix}~,

(3.2)

from which the quantity
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}
, defined in (
2.42
), in the present case reads

\begin{split}\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=3\mathfrak{c}_{1}+2\mathfrak{c}_{2}+\mathfrak{c}_{3}-1~.\end{split}

(3.3)

Any choices of
\mathfrak{c}_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
lead to the same Coulomb branch Hilbert series. However, if we would like to consider a specific discrete gauging, an appropriate choice must be made. We will shortly state our choices of
\mathfrak{c}_{i}
in subsequent calculations.

Let us define the function

\begin{split}f(\bm{m})=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathfrak{c}_{i}m_{i}\end{split}

(3.4)

as in (
2.43
), which takes values
0,1,\ldots,\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}
for given
\mathfrak{c}_{i}
. Then, the Coulomb branch Hilbert series of (
3.1
) can be obtained via the monopole formula (
2.51
) as follows:

\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})}\right](t,\bm{w})\\
&=\left(1-t^{2}\right)\sum_{j=0}^{\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}}\sum_{\bm{m}\in\frac{\Gamma_{G}^{mw}}{W_{G}}}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{3}P_{\mathrm{U}(1)}(m_{i},t^{2})w_{i}^{m_{i}}\right]\times t^{2\Delta(\bm{m})}\delta_{f(\bm{m}),j}~,\end{split}

(3.5)

where
w_{i}
are the topological fugacities associated with the three
\U(1)
gauge nodes, and
G=\widetilde{G}/\U(1)
with
\widetilde{G}=\U(1)^{3}
. Using (
3.2
), the conformal dimension appearing in (
3.5
) reads

\begin{split}2\Delta(\bm{m})=&\left|2m_{1}-3m_{2}\right|+\left|m_{1}-3m_{3}\right|+\left|m_{2}-2m_{3}\right|~,\end{split}

(3.6)

where it is important to take into account the constraint coming from the delta function
\delta_{f(\bm{m}),j}
.

A convenient choice to ungauge the decoupled
\U(1)
gauge group is to set
\mathfrak{c}_{1}=\mathfrak{c}_{2}=0
and
\mathfrak{c}_{3}=1
, such that
\lambda_{\mathfrak{c}}=0
and
f(\bm{m})=m_{3}
. Adopting this parametrisation, the conformal dimension is given by (
3.6
), with the constraint
m_{3}=0
. Upon setting the topological fugacities to unity, the Coulomb branch Hilbert series admits the following closed form:

\begin{split}\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})}\right](t,w_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1+t^{2}+3t^{3}+4t^{4}+4t^{5}+4t^{6}+3t^{7}+t^{8}+t^{10}}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)\left(1-t^{3}\right)\left(1-t^{4}\right)\left(1-t^{5}\right)}\\
&=1+2t^{2}+4t^{3}+7t^{4}+10t^{5}+16t^{6}+22t^{7}+31t^{8}+40t^{9}+54t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[2t^{2}+4t^{3}+4t^{4}+2t^{5}-6t^{6}-10t^{7}-12t^{8}+2t^{9}+29t^{10}+\ldots\right]~.\end{split}\end{split}

(3.7)

We give an algebraic description of this Coulomb branch by computing the equations for the Higgs branch of the mirror quiver in
3.1.2
.
Note that the Coulomb branch symmetry of the theory, which can be read from the moment map operators appearing at order
t^{2}
, is
\mathfrak{u}(1)^{2}
, reflecting that there are two independent
\U(1)
topological symmetries in theory (
3.1
). This is consistent with the relation (
2.52
).

Let us now demonstrate how to realise various
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
quotients, i.e. gauging
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
zero-form symmetries, which we will refer to as
\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{r}
.

\mathbb{Z}_{2}
quotient.

Suppose that we would like to perform a
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
quotient, i.e. gauge the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
zero-form symmetry. We can take
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(0,1,0)
and consider only the contribution of
j=0
in the first summation in (
3.5
). This amounts to setting
m_{2}=0
in (
3.5
). The resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is

\begin{split}\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{2}$}\right](t,w_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1+t^{2}+t^{3}+t^{4}+2t^{5}+3t^{6}+4t^{7}+3t^{8}+2t^{9}+t^{10}+t^{11}+t^{12}+t^{14}}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)\left(1-t^{3}\right)\left(1-t^{5}\right)\left(1-t^{8}\right)}\\
&=1+2t^{2}+2t^{3}+3t^{4}+6t^{5}+8t^{6}+12t^{7}+17t^{8}+20t^{9}+28t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[2t^{2}+2t^{3}+2t^{5}+t^{6}+2t^{7}-4t^{9}-5t^{10}+\ldots\right]~.\end{split}\end{split}

(3.8)

In this particular case, we obtain

\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})}\right]}{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{2}$}\right]}=2~,\end{split}

(3.9)

as expected from the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
quotient.

\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient.

This can be realised using
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(1,0,0)
and consider only the contribution of
j=0
in the first summation in (
3.5
). The resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is

\begin{split}\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3}$}\right](t,z_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1+t^{2}+2t^{4}+t^{5}+2t^{6}+3t^{7}+2t^{8}+3t^{9}+2t^{10}+t^{11}+2t^{12}+t^{14}+t^{16}}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)\left(1-t^{4}\right)\left(1-t^{5}\right)\left(1-t^{9}\right)}\\
&=1+2t^{2}+5t^{4}+2t^{5}+8t^{6}+6t^{7}+13t^{8}+14t^{9}+20t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[2t^{2}+2t^{4}+2t^{5}+2t^{7}-t^{8}-t^{10}+\ldots\right]~.\end{split}\end{split}

(3.10)

We also obtain

\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})}\right]}{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3}$}\right]}=3~,\end{split}

(3.11)

as expected from the
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient.

Another
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient.

We can also realise a
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient by setting
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(0,1,1)
and consider only the contribution of
j=0
in the first summation in (
3.5
). We point out that this
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient is not equivalent to the one presented above, as can be seen from the resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series, which does not coincide with (
3.10
):

\begin{split}\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3^{\prime}}$}\right](t,w_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1}{\left(1-t\right)\left(1-t^{2}\right)\left(1-t^{12}\right)\left(1-t^{15}\right)}\left(1-t+t^{2}+t^{3}-t^{4}+t^{5}+t^{6}-t^{7}\right.\\
&\left.\quad\,\,\,\,\,+3t^{8}+3t^{9}-t^{10}+3t^{11}+2t^{12}-2t^{13}+2t^{14}+\text{palindrome}+t^{26}\right)\\
&=1+2t^{2}+2t^{3}+3t^{4}+4t^{5}+6t^{6}+6t^{7}+11t^{8}+14t^{9}+18t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[2t^{2}+2t^{3}-t^{6}+2t^{8}+4t^{9}+2t^{10}+\ldots\right]~,\end{split}\end{split}

(3.12)

where, in order to avoid confusion with the previous
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient, we denote by
\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3^{\prime}}
the zero-form symmetry which is gauged in the present case. This
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient is consistent with

\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})}\right]}{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3^{\prime}}$}\right]}=3~.\end{split}

(3.13)

\mathbb{Z}_{13}
quotient.

This can be realised using
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(3,2,0)
and consider only the contribution of
j=0
in the first summation in (
3.5
). The resulting Coulomb branch Hilbert series is

\begin{split}\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{13}$}\right](t,w_{i}=1)\\
&=\frac{1}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)\left(1-t^{5}\right)\left(1-t^{39}\right)\left(1-t^{52}\right)}\left(1+t^{2}+t^{4}+t^{5}+t^{6}+t^{7}+t^{8}+t^{9}\right.\\
&\left.\quad\,\,\,\,\,+t^{10}+t^{11}+t^{12}+\ t^{13}+t^{14}+t^{15}+t^{16}+t^{17}+3t^{18}+5t^{19}+3t^{20}+5t^{21}\right.\\
&\left.\quad\,\,\,\,\,+5t^{22}+3t^{23}+3t^{24}+3t^{25}+3t^{26}+3t^{27}+3t^{28}+3t^{29}+3t^{30}+3t^{31}\right.\\
&\left.\quad\,\,\,\,\,+3t^{32}+3t^{33}+3t^{34}+5t^{35}+5t^{36}+7t^{37}+9t^{38}+8t^{39}+7t^{40}+6t^{41}\right.\\
&\left.\quad\,\,\,\,\,+5t^{42}+4t^{43}+4t^{44}+4t^{45}+4t^{46}+4t^{47}+4t^{48}+\text{palindrome}+t^{94}\right)\\
&=1+2t^{2}+3t^{4}+2t^{5}+4t^{6}+4t^{7}+5t^{8}+6t^{9}+8t^{10}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[2t^{2}+2t^{5}-t^{10}+\ldots\right]~.\end{split}\end{split}

(3.14)

We also obtain

\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})}\right]}{\mathrm{Vol}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{Trianglequivggg})/$\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{13}$}\right]}=13~,\end{split}

(3.15)

which is expected for a
\mathbb{Z}_{13}
quotient.

We will discuss such quotients, the resulting dual one-form symmetries and mixed ’t Hooft anomalies more systematically using the index.

3.1.1
Superconformal Index of Theory (
3.1
)

As described in Section
2.1.7
, an overall
\U(1)
in (
3.1
) can be modded out in many ways. In this subsection, we adopt the alternative method described around (
2.45
), which is more conventional for computing superconformal indices. In particular, we achieve this by restricting the gauge fugacities and the corresponding magnetic fluxes in the following way:

\begin{split}\prod_{i=1}^{3}z_{i}^{\mathfrak{c}_{i}}=1~,\quad\sum_{i=1}^{3}{\mathfrak{c}_{i}}m_{i}=0~,\end{split}

(3.16)

where we also allow the magnetic fluxes
m_{i}
to be non-integers. As we discussed earlier around (
2.45
), this amounts to reducing the freedom on
\sum_{i=1}^{3}{\mathfrak{c}_{i}}m_{i}
in (
3.4
) by setting it to zero, but increasing the freedom on the magnetic fluxes by allowing them to take non-integral values. We will soon discuss the conditions that determine the allowed values of
m_{i}
. We will also determine the discrete symmetry that acts on the monopole operators with fractional magnetic fluxes, refine it with an appropriate fugacity in the index, and eventually gauge it.

The superconformal index of theory (
3.1
) can be computed from the following expression:

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.92}{$\begin{split}{\cal I}_{\text{(\ref{Trianglequivggg})}}=&\sum_{m_{1},m_{2},m_{3}}w_{1}^{m_{1}}w_{2}^{m_{2}}w_{3}^{m_{3}}\oint\frac{dz_{1}}{2\pi iz_{1}}\oint\frac{dz_{2}}{2\pi iz_{2}}\oint\frac{dz_{3}}{2\pi iz_{3}}\,\,\delta\text{(\ref{constr0})}\times{\cal I}_{\text{matter}}~,\\
{\cal I}_{\text{matter}}=&\left[{\cal I}_{\chi}^{1}\left(a^{-2};0;x\right)\right]^{2}\times\prod_{s=\pm 1}{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left((z_{1}^{-1}z_{3}^{3})^{s}a;s(-m_{1}+3m_{3});x\right)\\
&\times{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left((z_{1}^{2}z_{2}^{-3}a)^{s};s(2m_{1}-3m_{2});x\right)\times{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left((z_{2}z_{3}^{-2})^{s}a;s(m_{2}-2m_{3});x\right)~,\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.17)

where the contribution of the chiral multiplet of
R
-charge
R
is

\begin{split}{\cal Z}^{R}_{\chi}(z;l;x)=\left(x^{1-R}z^{-1}\right)^{|l|/2}\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{1-(-1)^{l}z^{-1}x^{|l|+2-R+2j}}{1-(-1)^{l}z\,x^{|l|+R+2j}}~.\end{split}

(3.18)

For simplicity, we have turned off the background magnetic fluxes for the axial symmetry
a
and for the topological symmetries
w_{1,2,3}
. The notation
\delta\text{(\ref{constr0})}
means that we impose the constraint (
3.16
) upon integrating over the gauge fugacities and summing over the gauge fluxes. A set of conditions that needs to be satisfied in order to make the index well-defined is the Dirac quantisation conditions which require that the magnetic fluxes in the arguments of each factor
{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}
must be integers:

\begin{split}m_{1}-3m_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}~,\quad 2m_{1}-3m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}~,\quad m_{2}-2m_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}~.\end{split}

(3.19)

In (
3.17
), we sum the gauge magnetic fluxes
m_{i}
over all possible values (including the fractional ones) that are allowed by (
3.19
).

The conditions (
3.16
) allow us to write, for example,

\begin{split}z_{2}=z_{1}^{-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}}z_{3}^{-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}}~,\quad m_{2}=-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}m_{1}-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}m_{3}~,\quad\mathfrak{c}_{2}\neq 0~.\end{split}

(3.20)

Imposing these in the above index amounts to ungauge the overall
\U(1)
from the node associated with
m_{2}
. Using (
3.20
), we see that the Dirac quantisation conditions become

\begin{split}m_{1}-3m_{3}&\in\mathbb{Z}~,\\
\frac{3\mathfrak{c}_{1}+2\mathfrak{c}_{2}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}m_{1}+\frac{3\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}m_{3}&\in\mathbb{Z}~,\\
\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}m_{1}+\frac{2\mathfrak{c}_{2}+\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}m_{3}&\in\mathbb{Z}~.\end{split}

(3.21)

Due to the condition (
3.20
), we are left with two independent topological fugacities
v_{1}
and
v_{3}
that appear in the index as
v_{1}^{m_{1}}v_{3}^{m_{3}}
, where
10
10

10

The restriction of three topological fugacities to two was also achieved in (
2.52
) in a different way. In this case, we impose the condition (
3.16
) on the magnetic fluxes and then seek two independent combinations of topological fugacities which turn out to be
v_{1}
and
v_{3}
.

\begin{split}v_{1}=w_{1}w_{2}^{-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}}~,\quad v_{3}=w_{3}w_{2}^{-\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}}~.\end{split}

(3.22)

Suppose that the allowed magnetic fluxes in (
3.21
) include those with non-integral values and, upon writing them in the lowest terms, the largest denominator is
r
. This indicates the presence of a
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
zero-form magnetic symmetry that acts non-trivially on the monopole operators with fractional magnetic fluxes. In particular, whenever
m_{1}
or
m_{3}
is
not
an integer, if there is an integer linear combination of
m_{1}
and
m_{3}
such that

\begin{split}r(x_{1}m_{1}+x_{3}m_{3})\neq 0~({\rm mod}~r)~,\qquad\text{for some $x_{1},x_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}$}~,\end{split}

(3.23)

then the index can then be refined with respect to a discrete fugacity
g
associated with
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
such that
g^{r}=1
by inserting the factor

\begin{split}g^{r(x_{1}m_{1}+x_{3}m_{3})}\end{split}

(3.24)

inside the summation in (
3.17
). For convenience, we will refer to this
\mathbb{Z}_{r}
zero-form symmetry as
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
. Explicitly, the index (
3.17
) up to order
x^{2}
reads

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.89}{$\begin{split}{\cal I}_{\text{(\ref{Trianglequivggg})}}&=1+(a^{2}+2a^{-2})x+\left(g^{-2}u_{1}+g^{-1}u_{2}+gu_{2}^{-1}+g^{2}u_{1}^{-1}\right)a^{-3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}\\
&\quad\,\,\,\,\,+\left[a^{4}-4+\left(g^{-3}u_{1}u_{2}+g^{-1}u_{1}u_{2}^{-1}+3+gu_{1}^{-1}u_{2}+g^{3}u_{1}^{-1}u_{2}^{-1}\right)a^{-4}\right]x^{2}+\ldots~,\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.25)

where
u_{1}
and
u_{2}
are some functions of the topological fugacities
v_{1}
and
v_{3}
, and at least one of which, say
u_{2}
, takes the form
u_{2}=(v_{1}^{y_{1}}v_{3}^{y_{3}})^{\frac{1}{r}}
, with
y_{1}
and
y_{3}
integers coprime to
r
. Setting
g=1
and
u_{i}=1
, the Coulomb branch limit of (
3.25
) is in agreement with (
3.7
). We will discuss the Higgs branch below.

This refinement allows us to gauge
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
by summing
g
over all of the
r
-th roots of unity and dividing the result by
r
. After gauging, the resulting theory, which we refer to as (
3.1
)
/(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
, has a dual
\mathbb{Z}^{[1]}_{r}
one-form symmetry, denoted by
(\mathbb{Z}^{[1]}_{r})_{\widehat{g}}
. The fractional powers of
v_{1}
and
v_{3}
in
u_{2}=(v_{1}^{y_{1}}v_{3}^{y_{3}})^{\frac{1}{r}}
in the index of theory (
3.1
), in fact, imply the following mixed ’t Hooft anomaly in theory (
3.1
)
/(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
:

\begin{split}\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i}{r}\int_{M_{4}}B^{2}_{\widehat{g}}\cup\left[c_{1}(\U(1)_{v_{1}^{y_{1}}v_{3}^{y_{3}}})\,\,{\rm mod}\,\,r\right]\right)~,\end{split}

(3.26)

where
B^{(2)}_{\widehat{g}}
is the two-form background field for
(\mathbb{Z}^{[1]}_{2})_{\widehat{g}}
and
c_{1}(\U(1)_{v_{1}^{y_{1}}v_{3}^{y_{3}}})
is the first Chern-class associated with the linear combination
y_{1}\U(1)_{v_{1}}+y_{3}\U(1)_{v_{3}}
of the
\U(1)_{v_{1}}
and
\U(1)_{v_{3}}
topological symmetries associated with the fugacities
v_{1}
and
v_{3}
respectively. Here
M_{4}
is the 4d bulk such that
\partial M_{4}=M_{3}
, with
M_{3}
being the 3d spacetime in which the theory in question lives. Indeed, (
3.26
) manifests itself in the following way: upon gauging
(\mathbb{Z}^{[1]}_{r})_{\widehat{g}}
, we go back to theory (
3.1
) whose index contains the terms involving
(v_{1}^{y_{1}}v_{3}^{y_{3}})^{\frac{1}{r}}
, which contains an improper quantisation of the charge of
\U(1)_{v_{1}^{y_{1}}v_{3}^{y_{3}}}
. We will demonstrate this in the following examples below:

•

(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(0,1,0)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
,

•

(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(1,0,0)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
,

•

(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(0,1,1)
for another
\mathbb{Z}_{3}\equiv\mathbb{Z}_{3^{\prime}}
,

•

(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(3,2,0)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{13}
.

Let us briefly mention that one can take the Higgs and Coulomb branch limits of the index to obtain the Higgs and Coulomb branch Hilbert series
[
32
]
. In particular, we define

\begin{split}&h=x^{1/2}a~,~c=x^{1/2}a^{-1}~,\\
&\text{or equivalently}\quad x=hc~,~a=(h/c)^{1/2}~,\end{split}

(3.27)

and substitute them in the index. In the Higgs branch limit we send
c\rightarrow 0
and keep
h
fixed, whereas in the Coulomb branch limit we send
h\rightarrow 0
and keep
c
fixed. Note that, given a series expansion of the index in terms of
x
, the Higgs (
resp.
Coulomb) branch limit can be obtained by reading off the coefficients of the terms
a^{p}x^{\frac{p}{2}}
(
resp.

a^{-p}x^{\frac{p}{2}}
), with
p\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, and multiplying each of them to
h^{p}
(
resp.

c^{p}
). Conventionally, the corresponding Hilbert series can be obtained by simply setting
h
or
c
in each of the aforementioned limits to
t
.

The Coulomb branch limits of the indices of (
3.1
)
/(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
in these examples, upon setting
u_{i}=1
, are in agreement with the Coulomb branch Hilbert series (
3.8
), (
3.10
), (
3.12
) and (
3.14
), as expected.

On the other hand, the Higgs branch limit of the index (
3.25
) gives
\mathop{\rm PE}[t^{2}+2t^{6}-t^{12}]
. This indicates that the Higgs branch of (
3.1
) is isomorphic to
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{6}
. The generators are as follows:

\begin{split}G_{0}&=Q_{(0,1,-2)}\widetilde{Q}_{(0,1,-2)}=Q_{(-1,0,3)}\widetilde{Q}_{(-1,0,3)}=Q_{(2,-3,0)}\widetilde{Q}_{(2,-3,0)}~,\\
G_{+}&=Q_{(0,1,-2)}^{3}Q_{(-1,0,3)}^{2}Q_{(2,-3,0)}~,\\
G_{-}&=\widetilde{Q}_{(0,1,-2)}^{3}\widetilde{Q}_{(-1,0,3)}^{2}\widetilde{Q}_{(2,-3,0)}~,\end{split}

(3.28)

where we denote by
Q_{(q_{1},q_{2},q_{3})}
the chiral field that carries charges
(q_{1},q_{2},q_{3})
under the gauge groups labelled by
i=1,2,3
in (
3.1
), and by
\widetilde{Q}_{(q_{1},q_{2},q_{3})}
the chiral field in the same hypermultiplet with the opposite gauge charge. These generators satisfy the defining relation
G_{+}G_{-}=G_{0}^{6}
of
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{6}
, as expected. This moduli space is unaffected upon gauging the
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
zero-form symmetry. This can also be seen from the Higgs branch limit of the index (
3.25
): the coefficients of the terms
a^{p}x^{\frac{p}{2}}
, with
p\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, never contain
g
.

Example 1.
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(0,1,0)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{2}

The solutions to (
3.21
) form the two-dimensional lattices
\mathbf{\Lambda}_{p}=\left(\mathbb{Z}+\frac{p}{2}\right)^{2}
, with
p=0,1
. In (
3.23
), we can choose, for example,

and

, so that, when

in (

\begin{split}{\cal I}_{\text{(\ref{Trianglequivggg})}}=\sum_{p=0}^{1}\,\,\sum_{(m_{1},m_{3})\in\Lambda_{p}}\,\,g^{p}\,\,v_{1}^{m_{1}}v_{3}^{m_{3}}\oint\frac{dz_{1}}{2\pi iz_{1}}\oint\frac{dz_{3}}{2\pi iz_{3}}\left[{\cal I}_{\text{matter}}\right]_{\text{(\ref{constr1})}}~,\end{split}

(3.29)

where we denote by
\left[{\cal I}_{\text{matter}}\right]_{\text{(\ref{constr1})}}
the matter contribution in (
3.17
) subject to the constraint (
3.20
).
It can be easily seen that the fugacity

associated with the

is given in (

(3.30)

Gauging

)/

(3.31)

where the gauge magnetic fluxes are such that
(m_{1},m_{3})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}
.

Example 2.
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(1,0,0)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{3}

In this case, since
\mathfrak{c}_{2}=0
, in order to solve the conditions (
3.16
) in a valid way, we have to modify (
3.20
) by swapping
z_{1}\leftrightarrow z_{2}
,
\mathfrak{c}_{1}\leftrightarrow\mathfrak{c}_{2}
and
m_{1}\leftrightarrow m_{2}
. It then follows that we have two independent topological fugacities
v_{2}
and
v_{3}
appearing in the index as
v_{2}^{m_{2}}v_{3}^{m_{3}}
, which are defined by swapping the subscript
1
with the subscript
2
, and viceversa, in (
3.22
). Moreover, the Dirac quantisation conditions can be expressed as

\begin{split}m_{2}-2m_{3}&\in\mathbb{Z}~,\\
\frac{3\mathfrak{c}_{1}+2\mathfrak{c}_{2}}{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}m_{2}+\frac{2\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}m_{3}&\in\mathbb{Z}~,\\
\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{2}}{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}m_{2}+\frac{3\mathfrak{c}_{1}+\mathfrak{c}_{3}}{\mathfrak{c}_{1}}m_{3}&\in\mathbb{Z}~.\end{split}

(3.32)

In particular, for
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(1,0,0)
, these equations become

\begin{split}m_{2}-2m_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}~,\qquad 3m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}~,\qquad 3m_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}~.\end{split}

(3.33)

The solutions form the two-dimensional lattices
\mathbf{\Lambda}_{p}=(\mathbb{Z}+\frac{p}{3})\times(\mathbb{Z}-\frac{p}{3})
, with
p=0,1,2
. The index can be refined with a fugacity
g
by inserting the factor (
3.24
), with the substitution
x_{1}\rightarrow x_{2}
and
m_{1}\rightarrow m_{2}
. In particular, we can choose
x_{2}=1
and
x_{3}=0
such that, when
p=1,2
, a non-trivial power of
g
appears in the index (
3.17
). The explicit form of the index up to order
x^{2}
is given in (
3.25
) with

\begin{split}u_{1}=(v_{2}v_{3}^{-1})^{\frac{1}{3}}~,\qquad u_{2}=(v_{2}^{2}v_{3})^{\frac{1}{3}}~.\end{split}

(3.34)

Note that the index (
3.25
) can also be rewritten in terms of
u_{2}
and
integral
powers of
v_{2}
, since
u_{1}=v_{2}u_{2}^{-1}
. Gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{3}^{[0]})_{g}
leads to theory (
3.1
)/
(\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3})_{g}
with the mixed anomaly (
3.26
) with
r=3
,
y_{2}=2
and
y_{3}=1
.

We remark that (
3.1
)/
(\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3})_{g}
is also be described by the following quiver, which amounts to opening up the quiver (
3.1
) at node labelled by
m_{1}
:

(3.35)

where the gauge magnetic fluxes are such that
(m_{2},m_{3})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}
.

Example 3.
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(0,1,1)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{3^{\prime}}

Let us also examine another
\mathbb{Z}_{3}
quotient, which we previously denoted by
\mathbb{Z}_{3^{\prime}}
. In this case, the two-dimensional lattices which arise from solving the Dirac quantisation conditions (
3.21
) are given by
\mathbf{\Lambda}_{p}=\mathbb{Z}\times\left(\mathbb{Z}+\frac{p}{3}\right)
, with
p=0,1,2
. Therefore, we can choose
x_{1}=0
and
x_{3}=1
in (
3.23
) such that, when
p\neq 0
, the index is refined with a non-trivial power of
g
, given by (
3.24
). The explicit expression of the index up to order
x^{2}
is given by (
3.25
), with

\begin{split}u_{1}=g^{2}v_{1}~,\qquad u_{2}=v_{3}^{-\frac{1}{3}}~.\end{split}

(3.36)

It follows that, upon gauging
(\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3^{\prime}})_{g}
, we reach theory (
3.1
)/
(\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{3^{\prime}})_{g}
with the mixed anomaly given by (
3.26
) with
r=3
,
y_{1}=0
and
y_{3}=1
.

Example 4.
(\mathfrak{c}_{1},\mathfrak{c}_{2},\mathfrak{c}_{3})=(3,2,0)
for
\mathbb{Z}_{13}

Finally, let us consider the
\mathbb{Z}_{13}
discrete symmetry. The solutions to the conditions (
3.21
) form the two-dimensional lattices
\mathbf{\Lambda}_{p}=\left(\mathbb{Z}+\frac{p}{13}\right)\times\left(\mathbb{Z}-\frac{4p}{13}\right)
, with
p=0,\ldots,12
. We can choose
x_{1}=1
and
x_{3}=2
in (
3.23
) in such a way that, when
p\neq 0
, a non-trivial power of
g
, given by (
3.24
), appears in the index. Up to order
x^{2}
, the index is given explicitly by (
3.25
) with

\begin{split}u_{1}=(v_{1}^{4}v_{3}^{-3})^{\frac{1}{13}}~,\qquad u_{2}=(v_{1}^{2}v_{3}^{5})^{\frac{1}{13}}~.\end{split}

(3.37)

Note that the index (
3.25
) can also be rewritten in terms of
u_{2}
and
integral
powers of
v_{3}
, since
u_{1}=v_{3}^{-1}u_{2}^{2}
. Gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{13}^{[0]})_{g}
leads to theory (
3.1
)/
(\mathbb{Z}^{[0]}_{13})_{g}
with the mixed anomaly (
3.26
) with
r=13
,
y_{1}=2
and
y_{3}=5
.

3.1.2
Mirror Dual of Theory (
3.1
)

The 3d mirror of (
3.1
) is

(3.40)

The superpotential reads

W=\widetilde{Q}_{1}\Phi Q_{1}+\widetilde{Q}_{2}\Phi Q_{2}+\widetilde{Q}_{3}\Phi Q_{3}\;,

(3.41)

from which we obtain the
F
-term

F=\frac{\partial W}{\partial\Phi}=Q_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{1}+Q_{2}\widetilde{Q}_{2}+Q_{3}\widetilde{Q}_{3}\;.

(3.42)

The Higgs branch of (
3.38
).

Let us list the generators of the Higgs branch below. At degree 2, we have

\begin{split}A_{1}=\widetilde{Q}_{1}Q_{1}~,\qquad A_{2}=\widetilde{Q}_{2}Q_{2}~,\qquad A_{3}=\widetilde{Q}_{3}Q_{3}~,\end{split}

(3.43)

subject to the following relation coming from the
F
-term

\begin{split}A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3}=0~.\end{split}

(3.44)

At degree 3, we have

\begin{split}\begin{array}[]{ll}B_{1}=\widetilde{Q}_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{1}Q_{2}~,&\qquad B_{2}=Q_{1}Q_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{2}~,\\
B_{3}=\widetilde{Q}_{3}Q_{2}Q_{1}~,&\qquad B_{4}=Q_{3}\widetilde{Q}_{2}\widetilde{Q}_{1}~.\end{array}\end{split}

(3.45)

At degree 4, we have

\begin{split}\begin{array}[]{ll}C_{1}=\widetilde{Q}_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{1}Q_{3}~,&\qquad C_{2}=Q_{1}Q_{1}Q_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{3}~,\\
C_{3}=\widetilde{Q}_{1}\widetilde{Q}_{3}Q_{2}Q_{2}~,&\qquad C_{4}=Q_{1}Q_{3}\widetilde{Q}_{2}\widetilde{Q}_{2}~.\end{array}\end{split}

(3.46)

At degree 5, we have

\begin{split}D_{1}=\widetilde{Q}_{2}\widetilde{Q}_{2}\widetilde{Q}_{2}Q_{3}Q_{3}~,\qquad D_{2}=Q_{2}Q_{2}Q_{2}\widetilde{Q}_{3}\widetilde{Q}_{3}~.\end{split}

(3.47)

The relations are as follows. At degree 6, we have

\begin{split}\begin{array}[]{ll}B_{2}B_{4}-A_{1}C_{4}=0~,&\qquad B_{1}B_{4}-A_{2}C_{1}=0~,\\
B_{2}B_{3}-A_{2}C_{2}=0~,&\qquad B_{1}B_{3}-A_{1}C_{3}=0~,\\
A_{1}A_{2}A_{3}-B_{3}B_{4}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}^{2}A_{2}-B_{1}B_{2}=0~.\end{array}\end{split}

(3.48)

At degree 7, we have

\begin{split}\begin{array}[]{ll}B_{4}C_{4}-A_{1}D_{1}=0~,&\qquad B_{3}C_{3}-A_{1}D_{2}=0~,\\
A_{1}A_{2}B_{4}-B_{1}C_{4}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}^{2}B_{4}-B_{2}C_{1}=0~,\\
A_{1}A_{2}B_{3}-B_{2}C_{3}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}^{2}B_{3}-B_{1}C_{2}=0~,\\
A_{2}A_{3}B_{2}-B_{3}C_{4}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}A_{3}B_{2}-B_{4}C_{2}=0~,\\
A_{2}A_{3}B_{1}-B_{4}C_{3}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}A_{3}B_{1}-B_{3}C_{1}=0~.\\
\end{array}\end{split}

(3.49)

At degree 8, we have

\begin{split}\begin{array}[]{ll}C_{4}^{2}-B_{2}D_{1}=0~,&\qquad A_{2}A_{3}C_{4}-B_{3}D_{1}=0~,\\
C_{3}^{2}-B_{1}D_{2}=0~,&\qquad A_{2}A_{3}C_{3}-B_{4}D_{2}=0~,\\
A_{2}B_{4}^{2}-B_{1}D_{1}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}B_{4}^{2}-C_{1}C_{4}=0~,\\
A_{2}B_{3}B_{4}-C_{3}C_{4}=0~,&\qquad A_{2}B_{3}^{2}-B_{2}D_{2}=0~,\\
A_{1}B_{3}^{2}-C_{2}C_{3}=0~,&\qquad A_{3}B_{2}^{2}-C_{2}C_{4}=0~,\\
A_{3}B_{1}^{2}-C_{1}C_{3}=0~,&\qquad A_{1}^{3}A_{3}-C_{1}C_{2}=0~.\end{array}\end{split}

(3.50)

At degree 9, we have

\begin{split}\begin{array}[]{ll}A_{3}B_{2}C_{4}-C_{2}D_{1}=0~,&\qquad A_{3}B_{1}C_{3}-C_{1}D_{2}=0~,\\
B_{4}^{3}-C_{1}D_{1}=0~,&\qquad A_{2}^{2}A_{3}B_{4}-C_{3}D_{1}=0~,\\
B_{3}^{3}-C_{2}D_{2}=0~,&\qquad A_{2}^{2}A_{3}B_{3}-C_{4}D_{2}=0~.\\
\end{array}\end{split}

(3.51)

Finally, at degree 10, we have

\begin{split}A_{2}^{3}A_{3}^{2}-D_{1}D_{2}&=0~.\end{split}

(3.52)

Index of (
3.38
).

The index of this theory is given by

\begin{split}{\cal I}_{\text{(\ref{mirr123})}}=&\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}w^{m}\oint\frac{dz}{2\pi iz}{\cal I}_{\chi}^{1}(a^{-2};0;x)\times\Bigg[\prod_{s=\pm 1}{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left((gz)^{s};sm;x\right)\\
&\qquad\qquad\quad\,\,\,\times{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left((z^{2}u_{1})^{s};2sm;x\right)\times{\cal I}_{\chi}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left((z^{3}u_{1}u_{2})^{s};3sm;x\right)\Bigg]~,\end{split}

(3.53)

where
w
is the topological fugacity and
u_{1,2}
are the fugacities for the continuous
\U(1)^{2}
flavour symmetry. In the notation of (
3.40
), we assign
u_{1}^{\pm 1}
to
Q_{2}
and
\widetilde{Q}_{2}
and
(u_{1}u_{2})^{\pm 1}
to
Q_{3}
and
\widetilde{Q}_{3}
. As before we turn off the background magnetic fluxes for the global symmetries. In the above, we turn on the fugacity
g
(with
g^{r}=1
) associated with
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
symmetry. This turns out to act on
Q_{1}
and
\widetilde{Q}_{1}
as
g
and
g^{-1}
respectively. It is interesting to point out that, in theory (
3.1
), the
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
zero-form symmetry acts on the monopole operators via the gauge magnetic fluxes, whereas in the mirror theory (
3.39
) it acts on the chiral multiplets
Q_{1}
and
\widetilde{Q}_{1}
. This is consistent with mirror symmetry, in which the Higgs and Coulomb branches of the dual theories get exchanged.

To the first few orders in
x
, the index reads

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.91}{$\begin{split}{\cal I}_{\text{(\ref{mirr123})}}&=1+(a^{-2}+2a^{2})x+\left(g^{-2}u_{1}+g^{-1}u_{2}+gu_{2}^{-1}+g^{2}u_{1}^{-1}\right)a^{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}\\
&\quad\,\,\,\,\,+\left[a^{-4}-4+\left(g^{-3}u_{1}u_{2}+g^{-1}u_{1}u_{2}^{-1}+3+gu_{1}^{-1}u_{2}+g^{3}u_{1}^{-1}u_{2}^{-1}\right)a^{4}\right]x^{2}+\ldots\\
&=\text{(\ref{explicitindextriangle})}~\text{with $a\leftrightarrow a^{-1}$}~.\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.54)

The fact that the indices of (
3.39
) and (
3.1
) can be
equated upon exchanging
a
and
a^{-1}
supports the claim that these theories are indeed mirror dual. Gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
can be performed as before, namely by summing
g
over the
r
-th roots of unity and dividing by
r
. Since
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
acts on
Q_{1}
and
\widetilde{Q}_{1}
with the action
g
and
g^{-1}
(with
g^{r}=1
) respectively, such discrete gauging removes the Higgs branch generators (
3.43
)–(
3.47
) that carry non-trivial powers of
g
, i.e. those that are not neutral under
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
.

The Coulomb branch of (
3.38
).

Let us discuss the Coulomb branch of theory (
3.38
). Indeed, its Hilbert series is given by
\sum_{p\geq 0}c_{p}t^{2p}
, where
c_{p}
is given by the coefficient of the term
a^{-p}x^{\frac{p}{2}}
in index (
3.54
) (see
[
32
]
). The result is
\mathop{\rm PE}[t^{2}+2t^{6}-t^{12}]
, which is the Hilbert series of
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{6}
, in agreement with (
3.28
). The term
t^{2}
in the
\mathop{\rm PE}
corresponds to the generator
\Phi
, where
\Phi
is the adjoint field residing in the vector multiplet of the
\U(1)
gauge node in (
3.39
). The term
2t^{6}
in the
\mathop{\rm PE}
corresponds to the elementary monopole operators
V_{\pm}
with fluxes
\pm 1
in the
\U(1)
gauge node in (
3.39
). They satisfy the relation
V_{+}V_{-}=\Phi^{6}
, which is the defining relation of
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\mathbb{Z}_{6}
. Furthermore, we see that the Coulomb branch does not get affected by gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{r}^{[0]})_{g}
, since
g
appears only in the terms with positive power of
a
. This is in perfect agreement with the statement below (
3.28
) upon applying mirror symmetry.

(3.56)

the Coulomb branch Hilbert series can be obtained via the monopole formula (
2.51
), which in this case reads

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq22})}\right](t,\bm{w})=&\left(1-t^{2}\right)\sum_{\bm{m}\in\frac{\Gamma_{G}^{mw}}{W_{G}}}P_{\mathrm{U}(2)}(\bm{m}_{1},t^{2})\\
&\times\left[\prod_{i=2}^{4}P_{\mathrm{U}(1)}(m_{i},t^{2})w_{i}^{m_{i}}\right]t^{2\Delta(\bm{m})}\delta_{m_{1,1}+m_{1,2},0}~,\end{split}

(3.57)

where
w_{i}
, with
i=2,3,4
, are the topological fugacities associated with the three
\U(1)
nodes.
The adjacency matrix, rank vector and shortness vector associated with (
3.55
) are given respectively by

A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&2&1&1\\
2&-2&0&0\\
1&0&-2&0\\
1&0&0&-2\end{pmatrix}\,,\;v=\begin{pmatrix}2\\
1\\
1\\
1\end{pmatrix}\,,\;s=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
1\\
1\\
1\end{pmatrix}~,

(3.58)

from which, using (
2.32
), the conformal dimension appearing in (
3.57
) reads

\begin{split}2\Delta(\bm{m})=&-2\left|m_{1,1}-m_{1,2}\right|+2\left(\left|m_{1,1}-m_{2}\right|+\left|m_{1,2}-m_{2}\right|\right)\\
&\,\,+\left(\left|m_{1,1}-m_{3}\right|+\left|m_{1,2}-m_{3}\right|\right)+\left(\left|m_{1,1}-m_{4}\right|+\left|m_{1,2}-m_{4}\right|\right)~,\end{split}

(3.59)

with the constraint
m_{1,1}+m_{1,2}=0
coming from the delta function in (
3.57
). Explicitly, if we set the topological fugacities to unity, we obtain the following expression for the Coulomb branch Hilbert series:

\begin{split}\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq22})}\right](t,w_{i}=1)&=1+7t^{2}+56t^{4}+235t^{6}+843t^{8}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[7t^{2}+28t^{4}-45t^{6}-242t^{8}+\ldots\right]~,\end{split}\end{split}

(3.60)

which tells us that the Coulomb branch symmetry of the theory is
\mathfrak{su}(2)^{2}\oplus\mathfrak{u}(1)
.

Let us point out that quiver (
3.55
) possesses a
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}\times(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
one-form symmetry, where the
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}
factor is associated with the centre of the
\mathrm{SU}(2)
gauge group and
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
arises from the charge two
\U(1)
matter field.
11
11

11

As explained in
(
31
, Section 2)
(see also
(
34
, Appendices B and C)
), 3d
{\cal N}=4
SQED with two hypermultiplets of charge
q
possesses a
\mathbb{Z}_{q}
one-form symmetry, whose gauging leads to SQED with two hypermultiplets of charge one. As a direct consequence of this statement, gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
in theory (
3.55
) leads to (
3.61
).
The two
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
factors of the one-form symmetry can be gauged sequentially, giving rise to an interesting pattern of mixed ’t Hooft anomalies and global symmetry extensions.

(3.61)

whose Coulomb branch Hilbert series is given by (

A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&2&1&1\\
1&-2&0&0\\
1&0&-2&0\\
1&0&0&-2\end{pmatrix}\,,\;v=\begin{pmatrix}2\\
1\\
1\\
1\end{pmatrix}\,,\;s=\begin{pmatrix}1\\

1\\

(3.62)

) entering in the monopole formula (
3.57
) of quiver (
3.61
) reads

\begin{split}2\Delta(\bm{m})=&-2\left|m_{1,1}-m_{1,2}\right|+\left(\left|2m_{1,1}-m_{2}\right|+\left|2m_{1,2}-m_{2}\right|\right)\\
&\,\,+\left(\left|m_{1,1}-m_{3}\right|+\left|m_{1,2}-m_{3}\right|\right)+\left(\left|m_{1,1}-m_{4}\right|+\left|m_{1,2}-m_{4}\right|\right)~,\end{split}

(3.63)

with the constraint
m_{1,1}+m_{1,2}=0
. Upon setting

, the explicit expression of the Coulomb branch Hilbert series reads

\begin{split}\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq21})}\right](t,w_{i}=1)&=1+9t^{2}+88t^{4}+405t^{6}+1515t^{8}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[9t^{2}+43t^{4}-147t^{6}-538t^{8}+\ldots\right]~,\end{split}\end{split}

(3.64)

from which we observe that the Coulomb branch symmetry is
\mathfrak{su}(2)^{3}
. Alternatively, the same theory can be realised in an equivalent way by starting with quiver (
3.55
), with associated monopole formula (
3.57
) and conformal dimension (
3.59
), and explicitly gauge its
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
one-form symmetry by summing the magnetic flux
m_{2,1}
over half-integer values, i.e. we modify the summation over
m_{2}
in (
3.57
) as follows:

\begin{split}\sum_{m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}}\longrightarrow\sum_{p=0}^{1}y^{p}\sum_{m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{p}{2}}~,\end{split}

(3.65)

where
y
is the fugacity associated with the dual
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{y}
zero-form symmetry arising from gauging the one-form symmetry, such that
y^{2}=1
. This procedure allows us to refine the Coulomb branch Hilbert series of (
3.61
) with the fugacity
y
as follows:

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.98}{$\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq21})}\right](t,y,w_{i}=1)=1&+\left(7+2y\right)t^{2}+\left(56+32y\right)t^{4}\\
&+\left(235+170y\right)t^{6}+\left(843+672y\right)t^{8}+\ldots~.\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.66)

Observe that, if we sum (
3.66
) over
y=\pm 1
and divide by
2
, we recover (
3.60
):

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq22})}\right](t,\bm{w})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{y=\pm 1}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq21})}\right](t,y,\bm{w})~.\end{split}

(3.67)

This is consistent with the fact that theory (
3.55
) can be obtained upon gauging the
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{y}
symmetry of quiver (
3.61
).

(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}

For definiteness, let us pick the former choice of ungauging. The Coulomb branch Hilbert series reads

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq22})}\right](t,\bm{w})=&\left(1-t^{2}\right)\sum_{j=0,1}\sum_{\bm{m}\in\frac{\Gamma_{G}^{mw}}{W_{G}}}P_{\mathrm{U}(2)}(\bm{m}_{1},t^{2})w_{1}^{m_{1,1}+m_{1,2}}\\
&\times\left[\prod_{i=2}^{4}P_{\mathrm{U}(1)}(m_{i},t^{2})w_{i}^{m_{i}}\right]t^{2\Delta(\bm{m})}\delta_{m_{1,1}+m_{1,2},j}~,\end{split}

(3.69)

where
w_{1}
is the topological fugacity associated with the
\U(2)
gauge group and the conformal dimension is given by (
3.59
), with
m_{1,1}+m_{1,2}=\{0,1\}

\mathfrak{su}(4)
, denoted by
\overline{\mathrm{n.min}\,A_{3}}\cong\overline{\mathrm{n.min}\,D_{3}}
, see
(
35

:

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq22})}\right](t,w_{i}=1)&=\frac{\left(1+t^{2}\right)^{2}\left(1+5t^{2}+t^{4}\right)}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{8}}\\
&=1+15t^{2}+104t^{4}+475t^{6}+1659t^{8}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[15t^{2}-16t^{4}+35t^{6}-126t^{8}+\ldots\right]~.\end{split}

(3.70)

Indeed, it was formerly pointed out in

) coincides with the Hilbert series of

\begin{split}\sum_{m_{1,1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}\,\sum_{\left(m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\longrightarrow\sum_{q=0}^{1}x^{q}\sum_{m_{1,1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}+\frac{q}{2}}\,\sum_{\left(m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}\right)\in\left(\mathbb{Z}+\frac{q}{2}\right)^{3}}~,\end{split}

where we denote by

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.97}{$\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq22})}\right](t,x,w_{i}=1)=1&+\left(7+8x\right)t^{2}+\left(56+48x\right)t^{4}\\
&+\left(235+240x\right)t^{6}+\left(843+816x\right)t^{8}+\ldots~.\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.72)

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq21})}\right](t,w_{i}=1)&=\frac{\left(1+13t^{2}+28t^{4}+13t^{6}+t^{8}\right)}{\left(1-t^{2}\right)^{8}}\\
&=1+21t^{2}+168t^{4}+825t^{6}+3003t^{8}+\ldots\\
&=\mathop{\rm PE}\left[21t^{2}-63t^{4}+377t^{6}-2940t^{8}+\ldots\right]~.\end{split}

(3.75)

This can also be achieved directly from theory (
3.55
) by gauging the whole
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}\times(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
one-form symmetry at the level of the monopole formula by combining (
3.65
) and (
3.71
). Explicitly, we modify the summation in (
3.57
) as follows:

\begin{split}&\sum_{m_{1,1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}\,\sum_{\left(m_{2},m_{3},m_{4}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\\
&\longrightarrow\sum_{q=0}^{1}\sum_{p=0}^{1}x^{q}y^{p}\sum_{m_{1,1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}+\frac{q}{2}}\,\sum_{m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{q}{2}+\frac{p}{2}}\,\,\sum_{\left(m_{3},m_{4}\right)\in\left(\mathbb{Z}+\frac{q}{2}\right)^{2}}~.\end{split}

(3.76)

In this way, we can refine the Coulomb branch Hilbert series (
3.75
) with both
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
fugacities
x
and
y
:

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.96}{$\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq21})}\right](t,x,y,w_{i}=1)=1&+\left(7+8x+2y+4xy\right)t^{2}\\
&+\left(56+48x+32y+32xy\right)t^{4}\\
&+\left(235+240x+170y+180xy\right)t^{6}\\
&+\left(843+816x+672y+672xy\right)t^{8}+\ldots~,\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.77)

where we emphasise that the
\mathfrak{so}(7)
symmetry of (
3.74
) is manifest only when
x
and
y
are set to unity. Note that we can reproduce (
3.66
), (
3.72
) and (
3.60
) by gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{x}
,
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{y}
and
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{x}\times(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{y}
respectively, namely

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq21})}\right](t,y,\bm{w})&=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x=\pm 1}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq21})}\right](t,x,y,\bm{w})~,\end{split}

(3.78a)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq22})}\right](t,x,\bm{w})&=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{y=\pm 1}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq21})}\right](t,x,y,\bm{w})~,\end{split}

(3.78b)

\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLSU2pq22})}\right](t,\bm{w})&=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{x=\pm 1}\sum_{y=\pm 1}\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq21})}\right](t,x,y,\bm{w})~.\end{split}

(3.78c)

Observe that (
3.78b
) is consistent with the well-known result of
[
36
]
(see also
[
10
]
):

\begin{split}\overline{\mathrm{n.min}\,A_{3}}=\overline{\mathrm{min}\,B_{3}}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}~.\end{split}

(3.79)
