Mixed ’t Hooft anomalies

The Coulomb branch Hilbert series (
3.77
) turns out to be very interesting if, in addition to
x
and
y
, we also turn on the topological fugacities
w_{i}
. Let us focus on the coefficient appearing at order
t^{2}
of such Hilbert series:
14
14

14

For our purpose, it suffices to consider the coefficient of
t^{2}
in the Hilbert series. This is due to the fact that the Coulomb branch of the theory in question is
\overline{\mathrm{min}\,B_{3}}
, which has precisely one set of generators appearing at order
t^{2}
and transforming in the adjoint representation of
\mathfrak{so}(7)
; see also the last line of (
3.75
). As we will discuss below, upon turning on the fugacities
x
and
y
, the characters that are manifest in the Hilbert series are those of
\mathfrak{su}(2)_{w_{i}}
, with
i=2,3,4
.

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.97}{$\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}\left[\text{CB of (\ref{NSLU2pq21})}\right](t,x,y,\bm{w})\\
&=1+\left[3+w_{3}+w_{3}^{-1}+w_{4}+w_{4}^{-1}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}x\left(w_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{3}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{4}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)}\right.\\
&\left.\qquad\quad\quad+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}y\left(w_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.7,0.3}xy\left(w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{3}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{4}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)}\right]t^{2}+\ldots~,\end{split}$}\end{split}

(3.80)

where we highlight the topological fugacities appearing with half-integer powers in
blue
,
red
and
green
. Note that the
\mathrm{SO}(7)
flavour symmetry is manifest in the Hilbert series as the
\U(1)_{w_{2}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}}
subgroup.
15
15

15

Naively, the character that appears in (
3.80
) might seem to be that of
\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{2}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}}
, but this does not fit into the branching rule
\mathbf{21}\rightarrow(\mathbf{3},\mathbf{2},\mathbf{2})\oplus(\mathbf{3},\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{3},\mathbf{1})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1},\mathbf{3})
of
\mathrm{SO}(7)\rightarrow\mathrm{SU}(2)^{3}
. In fact, we see that the first
\mathrm{SU}(2)
factor in the aforementioned branching rule is broken to
\U(1)_{w_{2}}
and we have to further use the branching rule
\mathbf{3}\rightarrow(2)\oplus(0)\oplus(-2)
of
\mathrm{SU}(2)\rightarrow\U(1)_{w_{2}}
. We see that, in this convention, the normalisation for
w_{2}
is such that
w_{2}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}
corresponds to the
\U(1)_{w_{2}}
charge
\pm 2
.
The normalisations of the fugacities are as follows:
w_{2}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}
corresponds to the
\U(1)_{w_{2}}
charge
\pm 2
,
16
16

16

See Footnote
15
for the convention.
and, for
\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{i}}
(with
i=3,4
), the character of the fundamental representation is
w_{i}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
and that of the adjoint representation is
1+w_{i}+w_{i}^{-1}
.

The product of the brackets in
green
, namely
\left(w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{3}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{4}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)
, corresponds to
(\mathbf{2};\mathbf{2})
representation of
\left[\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}}\right]/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, where the quotient by
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
indicates the action that there is one independent combination of the centres of
\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}
and
\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}}
that acts trivially. Specifically, the aforementioned
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
acts by
\left(w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow-w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}},\,w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow-w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
simultaneously. On the other hand, the product of the brackets in
blue
, namely
\left(w_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{2}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{3}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}+w_{4}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)
, corresponds to the
(\mathbf{2};\mathbf{2})(2)\oplus(\mathbf{2};\mathbf{2})(-2)
representation of
\left[\U(1)_{w_{2}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}}\right]/(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})
, where the quotient by
\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
indicates that there are two independent combinations of the centres of
\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3,4}}
and
\U(1)_{w_{2}}
that act trivially. Specifically, the action of this
\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}
can be taken as
\left(w_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow-w_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}},\,w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow-w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
and
\left(w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow-w_{3}^{\frac{1}{2}},\,w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow-w_{4}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)
.

The terms in colour in (
3.80
) indicate the following mixed ’t Hooft anomalies (see for instance
[
37
,
31
,
38
,
39
,
40
]
).

•

The
red
terms in (
3.80
) indicate that gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
, which leads to the dual symmetry
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{y}
, gives rise to the half-integral power in
w_{2}^{\pm\frac{1}{2}}
. Indeed, the smallest magnitude of the
\U(1)_{w_{2}}
charge that appears in the Hilbert series is
2
. This means that there is a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly characterised by the following anomaly theory:

\begin{split}\exp\left(i\pi\int_{M_{4}}B^{(2)}_{y}\cup\left[c_{1}(\U(1)_{w_{2}})\,\,{\rm mod}\,\,2\right]\right)~,\end{split}

(3.81)

where
B^{(2)}_{y}\in H^{2}(M_{3},\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})
is the two-form background field for the
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
one-form symmetry, and
c_{1}(\U(1)_{w_{2}})
is the first Chern-class associated with the
\U(1)_{w_{2}}
symmetry. Here,
M_{4}
is the 4d bulk such that
\partial M_{4}=M_{3}
, with
M_{3}
being the 3d spacetime in which the theory in question lives.

•

Similarly, the terms highlighted in
blue
in (
3.80
) indicate that gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}
, which leads to the dual
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{x}
symmetry, is in conflict with the global form of the symmetry
(\U(1)_{w_{2}}/\mathbb{Z}_{2})\times\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{4}}
, due to the presence of the representation
(\mathbf{2};\mathbf{2})(2)\oplus(\mathbf{2};\mathbf{2})(-2)
. Thus, there is a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly characterised by the following anomaly theory:

\begin{split}\exp\left(i\pi\int_{M_{4}}B^{(2)}_{x}\cup\mathfrak{v}_{2}\right)~,\end{split}

(3.82)

where
B^{(2)}_{x}\in H^{2}(M_{3},\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})
is the two-form background field associated with the
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}
one-form symmetry, and
\mathfrak{v}_{2}
is the second Stiefel-Whitney class that obstructs the lift of the
(\U(1)_{w_{2}}/\mathbb{Z}_{2})\times\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{4}}
bundle to the
(\U(1)_{w_{2}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}})/(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2})
bundle.

•

Finally, for the
green
terms in (
3.80
), the fugacity
xy
corresponds to the diagonal subgroup of
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{x}\times(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{y}
, which we will denote by
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[0]})_{xy}
. The dual one-form symmetry is the diagonal subgroup of
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}}\times(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{y}}
which we will denote by
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}\widehat{y}}
. Gauging
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}\widehat{y}}
is in conflict with the global form of the symmetry
\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{4}}
, due to the presence of the representation
(\mathbf{2};\mathbf{2})
. This signals that there is a mixed ’t Hooft anomaly characterised by

\begin{split}\exp\left(i\pi\int_{M_{4}}B^{(2)}_{xy}\cup\mathfrak{w}_{2}\right)~,\end{split}

(3.83)

where
B^{(2)}_{xy}
is the two-form background field associated with the
(\mathbb{Z}_{2}^{[1]})_{\widehat{x}\widehat{y}}
one-form symmetry, and
\mathfrak{w}_{2}
is the second Stiefel-Whitney class that obstructs the lift of the
\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SO}(3)_{w_{4}}
bundle to the
(\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{3}}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{w_{4}})/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
bundle. Note that this mixed anomaly does not involve the topological symmetry associated with
w_{2}
.

4
Moduli Space of
B_{n}
Instantons via Discrete Gauging

4.1
\overline{\min B_{n}}
via Discrete Gauging

In this section, we present a method for obtaining the Hilbert series of the minimal nilpotent orbit closure of
B_{n}
, denoted by
\overline{\min B_{n}}
, by means of discrete gauging. So far in the literature, this has been obtained in two ways. The first way is from the
\USp(2)
gauge theory with
\frac{1}{2}(2n+1)
flavours. Since the number of flavours is not integral, in order for the theory to be consistent, the
\USp(2)
gauge group must possess a half-integral Chern-Simons level. The latter reduces the amount of supersymmetry and lifts the Coulomb branch. In this approach,
\overline{\min B_{n}}
should be regarded as a subvariety of the total moduli space of vacua of the supersymmetric Chern-Simons theory with vanishing expectation values for monopole operators. The second way is to apply the Coulomb branch formula
[
12
]
to the following affine
B_{n}
quiver with the prescription described in
[
6
]
:

(4.1)

4.1
) does not possess a conventional Lagrangian description, due to the presence of the non-simply laced edge. In the following, we provide an alternative approach to realise the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit of
B_{n}
involving only 3d
{\cal N}=4
theories with a Lagrangian description.

{\cal N}=4

gauge theory with
\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(2n+1\right)+m\right]
flavours, where

is odd.

(4.4)

where each line connecting
\mathbb{Z}_{m}
and
\USp(2)
denotes a half-hypermultiplet in the representation
(e^{2\pi i/m};\mathbf{2})
of
\mathbb{Z}_{m}\times\USp(2)
.

Our main claim is that, upon taking the limit
m\rightarrow\infty
, the Higgs branch of theory (
4.4
) is the closure of the minimal nilpotent orbit of
B_{n}
. In other words, we propose a realisation of the transition between the following nilpotent orbits:

\begin{split}\overline{\min\,D_{(2n+1+m)/2}}\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\overline{\min\,B_{n}}~.\end{split}

(4.5)

Let us also emphasise that, for each
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{m\geq 1}
(with
m
odd), the Higgs branch moduli space is a
(2m+n-2)
quaternionic dimensional hyperKähler cone, whose Hilbert series has a palindromic numerator. The Coulomb branch of theory (
4.4
) is isomorphic to
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\widehat{D}_{(2n+1+m)/2}
, which is actually the Coulomb branch of the orginal theory (
4.2
). We subsequently demonstrate these claims using the superconformal index and Hilbert series.

The index of theory (
4.4
) is given by

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.98}{$\begin{split}&{\cal I}_{(\ref{BnZm})}(\bm{f},\bm{m}|a,n_{a};x)\\
&=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l\in\mathbb{Z}}\oint\frac{dz}{2\pi iz}{\cal Z}^{\USp(2)}_{\text{vec}}\left(z;l;x\right)\prod_{s={0,\pm 1}}{\cal Z}^{1}_{\chi}\left(z^{2s}a^{-2};2sl-2n_{a};x\right)\\
&\qquad\times\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\prod_{s^{\prime}=\pm 1}\left[{\cal Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}\left(e^{\frac{2\pi i}{m}j}z^{s^{\prime}}a;s^{\prime}l+n_{a};x\right)\right]^{m}\\
&\qquad\times\prod_{s_{1}=\pm 1}{\cal Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}\left(z^{s_{1}}a;s_{1}l+n_{a};x\right)\prod_{s_{2}=\pm 1}\prod_{i=1}^{n}{\cal Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}\left(z^{s_{1}}f_{i}^{s_{2}}a;s_{1}l+s_{2}m_{i}+n_{a};x\right)~,\end{split}$}\end{split}

(4.6)

where the
\USp(2)
vector multiplet contribution is

\begin{split}&{\cal Z}^{\USp(2)}_{\text{vec}}(z;l;x)={x^{-{\left|2l\right|}}}\prod_{{s}={\pm{1}}}{\left({1}-{\left(-{1}\right)^{2{s}{l}}}{z^{2s}}{x^{2\left|{s}{l}\right|}}\right)}~.\end{split}

(4.7)

For
m\geq 3
and a general value of
n
, upon setting the background fluxes for the flavour symmetry and for the axial symmetry, i.e.
\bm{m}
and
n_{a}
respectively, to zero, the series expansion of the index up to order
x^{2}
reads

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.92}{$\begin{split}&{\cal I}_{(\ref{BnZm})}(\bm{f}|a;x)=1+\left[\chi^{B_{n}}_{[0,1,0,\ldots,0]}(\bm{f})a^{2}\right]x\\
&\quad\,\,\,\,\,+\left[\left(\chi^{B_{n}}_{[0,2,0,\ldots,0]}(\bm{f})+R\right)a^{4}+\left(1+r\right)a^{-4}-\left(1+\chi^{B_{n}}_{[0,1,0,\ldots,0]}(\bm{f})+m^{2}\right)\right]x^{2}+\ldots~,\end{split}$}\end{split}

(4.8)

where

\begin{split}R=\begin{cases}8\chi^{B_{n}}_{[1,0,\ldots,0]}(\bm{f})&\quad m=3\\
0&\quad m\geq 5\end{cases}~\quad\text{and}\quad r=\begin{cases}1&\quad n=2,m=3\\
0&\quad\text{otherwise}\end{cases}~.\end{split}

(4.9)

This has many interesting features which we now explain. At order
x
, we see that the continuous flavour symmetry of theory (
4.4
) is indeed
\mathfrak{so}(2n+1)
, whose fugacities are
\bm{f}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n})
. We therefore do not refine the fugacities with respect to the
m
bifundamental half-hypermultiplets in the gauge group
\mathbb{Z}_{m}\times\USp(2)
, whose contribution is denoted in the second line of (
4.6
). Note, however, that the contributions to the negative terms at order
x^{2}
are as follows:

•

1
: the
\U(1)_{a}
axial symmetry current,

•

\chi^{B_{n}}_{[0,1,0,\ldots,0]}
: the
\mathfrak{so}(2n+1)
flavour curents, and

•

m^{2}
: the conserved currents from the
\mathbb{Z}_{m}
discrete gauging of
m
hypermultiplets.
17
17

17

The index of the
\mathbb{Z}_{m}
discrete gauging of
m
hypermultiplets can be written in terms of
\mathfrak{su}(m)\times\mathfrak{u}(1)
representations as

\begin{split}&\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}(e^{\frac{2\pi i}{m}j}y^{-1}_{i},0;x)\,\mathbb{Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}(e^{-\frac{2\pi i}{m}j}y_{i},0;x)=1+\left(1+[1,0,\ldots,0,1]_{0}\right)x\\
&\qquad+\left\{[2,0,\ldots,0,2]_{0}-\left(1+[1,0,\ldots,0,1]_{0}\right)\right\}x^{2}+\left([n,0,\ldots,0]_{+n}+[0,\ldots,0,n]_{-n}\right)x^{n/2}+\ldots~,\end{split}

where
\mathbf{R}_{r}
denotes the
\mathfrak{su}(m)
character representation
\mathbf{R}
with
\mathfrak{u}(1)
charge
r
. Observe that the negative terms at order
x^{2}
are of dimension
1+(m^{2}-1)=m^{2}
, as required. This expression can also be obtained by starting from the index of
m
hypermultiplets, namely
\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}(y^{-1}_{i},0;x)\,\mathbb{Z}^{1/2}_{\chi}(y_{i},0;x)
, and then projecting out all representations of
\mathfrak{su}(m)
except those with
N
-ality
m
, i.e. those with the Young diagram with the number of boxes equal to zero modulo
m
.

The representations
[0,p,0,\ldots,0]
that appear as coefficients of
a^{2p}x^{p}
in the index precisely agree with those appearing in the Hilbert series of
\overline{\min B_{n}}

[
28
]
:

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\overline{\min B_{n}}\right](t,\bm{f})=\sum_{p=0}^{\infty}\chi^{B_{n}}_{[0,p,0,\ldots,0]}(\bm{f})t^{2p}~.\end{split}

(4.10)

For the special case of
m=3
, the additional gauge invariant operators that contribute
8\chi^{B_{n}}_{[1,0,\ldots,0]}(\bm{f})
correspond to
\epsilon^{ab}\epsilon^{cd}Q^{i}_{a}q^{(\alpha_{1})}_{b}q^{(\alpha_{2})}_{c}q^{(\alpha_{3})}_{d}
, where
i=1,\ldots,2n+1
,
a,b,c,d=1,2
, and
\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}=1,2,3
.
18
18

18

The multiplicity
8
can be seen as follows. The tensor
\epsilon^{cd}
imposes the antisymmetrisation of the indices
\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}
, and so
(\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})
can be taken as
(1,2)
,
(1,3)
,
(2,3)
. On the other hand,
\alpha_{1}
runs over
1,2,3
, and so we have
3\times 3=9
components that are subject to the identity
0=\epsilon_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}}q^{(\alpha_{1})}_{b}q^{(\alpha_{2})}_{c}q^{(\alpha_{3})}_{d}
(since
b,c,d=1,2
). The latter implies that
\epsilon^{bc}\left(q^{(1)}_{a}q^{(2)}_{b}q^{(3)}_{c}-q^{(2)}_{a}q^{(1)}_{b}q^{(3)}_{c}+q^{(3)}_{a}q^{(1)}_{b}q^{(2)}_{c}\right)=0
. We thus have 8 components, namely
(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3})=

\left\{(1,1,2)\right.
,
(2,1,2)
,
(3,1,2)
,
(1,1,3)
,
(2,1,3)
,
(3,1,3)
,
(2,2,3)
,
\left.(3,2,3)\right\}
.
Here,
Q^{i}_{a}
denotes the half-hypermultiplets in the bifundamental representation of
\USp(2)\times\mathrm{SO}(2n+1)
, and
q^{(\alpha_{j})}_{a}
denotes the half-hypermultiplets in the bifundamental representation of
\mathbb{Z}^{(j)}_{m}\times\USp(2)
. Finally, the term
a^{-4}
at order
x^{2}
corresponds to the Coulomb branch operator
\mathop{\rm tr}(\varphi^{2})
, where
\varphi
is the complex scalar in the
\USp(2)
vector multiplet. We remark that, for the special case of
n=2
and
m=3
, as will be seen in (
4.12
), we have a monopole operator with dimension two that contributes an extra term
a^{-4}x^{2}
to the index.

From (
3.27
), we see that, upon setting
h=t
, the Higgs branch limit of the index (
4.6
) gives rise to the following Hilbert series:

\begin{split}\begin{split}&\mathrm{HS}[\text{HB of (\ref{BnZm})}](t,\bm{f})\\
&=\oint_{|z|=1}\frac{dz}{2\pi iz}(1-z^{2})\times{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\left(\mathop{\rm PE}\left[(z+z^{-1})e^{\frac{2\pi i}{m}j}t\right]\right)^{m}}\\
&\qquad\times\mathop{\rm PE}\left[(z+z^{-1})\left\{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(f_{i}+f_{i}^{-1}\right)\right\}t-\left(z^{2}+1+z^{-2}\right)t^{2}\right]~,\end{split}\end{split}

(4.11)

Note that the blue terms are effectively the contribution of
m
hypermultiplets, each carrying charge
+1
under
\mathbb{Z}_{m}
. Since the total charge is
m\equiv 0\,({\rm mod}\,\,m)
, we expect that gauging the
\mathbb{Z}_{m}
symmetry preserves the hyperKähler structure, and so the Hilbert series is expected to have a palindromic numerator for every
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
and
m
odd. We also point out that the blue term approaches 1 as
m\rightarrow\infty
and so, in this limit, the integral reproduces the Hilbert series (
4.10
) as expected.

On the other hand, the Coulomb branch limit gives the monopole formula of the original theory (
4.2
), namely that of the
\USp(2)
gauge theory with
\frac{1}{2}(2n+1+m)
flavours. The is explicitly given in
(
12
, Section 5.2)
. The Coulomb branch of (
4.4
) is therefore
\mathbb{C}^{2}/\widehat{D}_{(2n+1+m)/2}
. As
m\rightarrow\infty
, the Coulomb branch Hilbert series simply reduces to
\mathop{\rm PE}[t^{4}]=(1-t^{4})^{-1}
, with
t=c
.

We demonstrate these statements explicitly in the case of
n=2
below.

4.1.1
The Case of
n=2

Let us focus on the example of
n=2
. We provide explicit expressions of the indices of (
4.4
) for
m=3,5,7
below.
19
19

19

Below we set
f_{i}=1
and
m_{i}=n_{a}=0
for convenience.

\begin{split}\begin{tabular}[]{c|l}\hline\cr$n=2$ and $m=$&\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad index of (\ref{BnZm})\\
\hline\cr$3$&$1+10a^{2}x+\left(75a^{4}+{2}{a^{-4}}-20\right)x^{2}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,+\left(674a^{6}+{a^{-6}}-235a^{2}-{10}{a^{-2}}\right)x^{3}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,+\left(3023a^{8}+169+{3}{a^{-8}}-1791a^{4}-{10}{a^{-4}}\right)x^{4}+\ldots$\\
\hline\cr$5$&$1+10a^{2}x+\left(35a^{4}+{a^{-4}}-36\right)x^{2}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,+\left(959a^{6}+{a^{-6}}-669a^{2}-{25}{a^{-2}}\right)x^{3}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,+\left(13010a^{8}+593+{2}{a^{-8}}-1924a^{4}-{26}{a^{-4}}\right)x^{4}+\ldots$\\
\hline\cr$7$&$1+10a^{2}x+\left(35a^{4}+{a^{-4}}-60\right)x^{2}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,+\left(84a^{6}-1245a^{2}-{49}{a^{-2}}\right)x^{3}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,+\left(23685a^{8}+1709+{2}{a^{-8}}-5828a^{4}-{49}{a^{-4}}\right)x^{4}+\ldots$\\
\hline\cr\end{tabular}\end{split}

(4.12)

The coefficient
10
in
10a^{2}x
corresponds to the adjoint representation
[0,2]
of
B_{2}
. For
m=3
, the coefficient
75
in
75a^{4}x^{2}
corresponds to
[0,4]+8[1,0]
. The negative terms at order
x^{2}
for a generic value of
m
is equal to
-1-10-m^{2}
. These are in accordance with the general statement presented above.

The Higgs branch Hilbert series of (
4.4
) can be computed as in (
4.11
) or simply by reading off the coefficients of the terms
a^{2p}x^{p}
(with
p=0,1,2,\ldots
) in the index.

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.9}{$\begin{tabular}[]{c|l}\hline\cr$n=2$ and $m=$&\qquad\qquad\quad Higgs branch Hilbert series of (\ref{BnZm})\\
\hline\cr 3&$\frac{1}{(1-t)^{10}(1+t)^{10}\left(1-t+t^{2}\right)^{6}\left(1+t+t^{2}\right)^{6}}$\\
&$\times\left(1+t^{2}\right)(1+5t^{2}+36t^{4}+388t^{6}+314t^{8}+1773t^{10}+3055t^{12}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,+1421t^{14}+6426t^{16}+1421t^{18}+\text{palindrome}+t^{32})$\\
&$=1+10t^{2}+75t^{4}+674t^{6}+3023t^{8}+10671t^{10}+\ldots$\\
\hline\cr 5&$\frac{1}{(1-t)^{14}(1+t)^{14}(1-t+t^{2}-t^{3}+t^{4})^{8}(1+t+t^{2}+t^{3}+t^{4})^{8}}$\\
&$\times(1+t^{2})(1+3t^{2}-13t^{4}+892t^{6}+6704t^{8}-5144t^{10}+21884t^{12}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,+197616t^{14}-29371t^{16}+285351t^{18}+877263t^{20}+769373t^{22}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,+2300312t^{24}+619674t^{26}+3913260t^{28}+5787010t^{30}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,+3453595t^{32}+5569730t^{34}+5062175t^{36}+9370620t^{38}$\\
&$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,+5062175t^{40}+\text{palindrome}+t^{76})$\\
&$=1+10t^{2}+35t^{4}+959t^{6}+13010t^{8}+65799t^{10}+\ldots$\\
\hline\cr 7&$1+10t^{2}+35t^{4}+84t^{6}+23685t^{8}+358966t^{10}+\ldots$\end{tabular}$}\end{split}

(4.13)

In the case of
m=7
, the closed form is complicated and so we report only the series expansion in
t
up to order
10
. It is instructive to compare these results with the Hilbert series of
\overline{\min\,B_{2}}
:

\begin{split}\mathrm{HS}\left[\overline{\min\,B_{2}}\right]&=\frac{1+6t^{2}+t^{4}}{(1-t)^{4}(1+t)^{4}}\\
&=1+10t^{2}+35t^{4}+84t^{6}+165t^{8}+286t^{10}+\ldots~.\end{split}

(4.14)

From the above, we see that the Higgs branch Hilbert series of (
4.4
) with for a given
m
reproduces (
4.14
) correctly up to order
t^{m-1}
.

The Coulomb branch Hilbert series can be obtained by reading off the coefficients of the terms
a^{-2p}x^{p}
(with
p=0,1,2,\ldots
) in the index.

\begin{split}\scalebox{0.97}{$\begin{tabular}[]{c|c|c}\hline\cr$n=2$ and $m=$&Coulomb branch Hilbert series of (\ref{BnZm})&Coulomb branch\\
\hline\cr 3&$1+2t^{4}+t^{6}+3t^{8}+2t^{10}+\ldots$&$\mathbb{C}^{2}/\widehat{D}_{4}$\\
&$=\mathop{\rm PE}[2t^{4}+t^{6}-t^{12}]$\\
\hline\cr 5&$1+t^{4}+t^{6}+2t^{8}+t^{10}+\ldots$&$\mathbb{C}^{2}/\widehat{D}_{5}$\\
&$=\mathop{\rm PE}[t^{4}+t^{6}+t^{8}-t^{16}]$\\
\hline\cr 7&$1+t^{4}+2t^{8}+t^{10}+2t^{12}+\ldots$&$\mathbb{C}^{2}/\widehat{D}_{6}$\\
&$=\mathop{\rm PE}[t^{4}+t^{8}+t^{10}-t^{20}]$\\
\end{tabular}$}\end{split}

(4.15)

(A.6)

These orbits are the magnetic lattice
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
of the true gauge group
G=\widetilde{G}/\mathrm{U}(1)
.

We can parametrise
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
in many different ways. We will show a few of these here

1.

Fix
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}0}
. Let us depict the points in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying the constraint as red dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as red lines:

(A.7)

We can see that every
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbit in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
is represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
. Note that fixing
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}=a
for any
a\in\mathbb{Z}
works just as well.

2.

{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}0}

\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying the constraint as blue dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as blue lines:

(A.8)

We can see that every
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbit in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
is represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
. Note that, just like before, fixing
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}=a
for any
a\in\mathbb{Z}
works just as well.

3.

Fix
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}\in\{{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}1}\}
. This is a more interesting case.

\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
are represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
.

Note that fixing
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}\in\{a,b\}
for any
a,b\in\mathbb{Z}
with
a
even and
b
odd works as well.

4.

Fix
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}\in\{{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}1},{\color[rgb]{0,1,1}2}\}
.

Let us first depict the points in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}={\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}
as orange dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as orange lines:

(A.12)

\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
are represented.

\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as purple lines:

(A.15)

where all
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
are represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
.

Note that fixing
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}\in\{a,b,c\}
for any
a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}
with
(a\;{\rm mod}\;3)=0
,
(b\;{\rm mod}\;3)=1
, and
(c\;{\rm mod}\;3)=2
works just as well.

5.

Now, consider a constraint on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}
. Since
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}=0
is equivalent to
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}=0
,
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}\in\{0\}
is a fine constraint. However one could also use the constraint
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}\in\{0,1\}
. Observe that
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}=1
implies
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}=\frac{1}{2}
, and, since
({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\frac{1}{2}},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}})\notin\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
, there is no additional contribution coming from
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}=1
.

It may seem silly to use the constraint
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}\in\{0,1\}
over
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}\in\{0\}
. We discuss it here to explain why the general formula (
2.43
) applies even in such boundary cases.

6.

Similarly, consider a constraint on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2m_{2}}
. Note that
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2m_{2}}\in\{0,1,2,3\}
is equivalent to
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2m_{2}}\in\{0,2\}
, which is equivalent to
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m_{2}}\in\{0,1\}
, which is a valid constraint as discussed before.

We discuss the constraint
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}2m_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2m_{2}}\in\{0,1,2,3\}
, since it agrees with the general formula (
2.43
).

A.2
Example 2: Single U(2) Node

Let us consider a single
\U(2)
gauge node

2
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}

(A.16)

with magnetic weights
({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}})\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}(2)}^{mw}
of the naive gauge group
\widetilde{G}=\mathrm{U}(2)
.
The Weyl group of
\widetilde{G}=\mathrm{U}(2)
is

W_{\mathrm{U}(2)}=S_{2}=\mathbb{Z}_{2}

(A.17)

and we may parametrise
\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}(2)}^{mw}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
by setting

-\infty<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}\leq{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}<\infty\;.

(A.18)

We depict the region of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}
with an orange shading, and the region of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}<{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}
with a lighter orange shading:

(A.19)

The adjacency matrix
A
, rank vector
v
and shortness vector
s
are given by

A=\begin{pmatrix}-2\end{pmatrix}\;,\hskip 10.00002ptv=\begin{pmatrix}2\end{pmatrix}\;,\hskip 10.00002pts=\begin{pmatrix}1\end{pmatrix}\;.

(A.20)

The conformal dimension (
2.32
) is then

2\Delta({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}})=-2|{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}-{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}|\;.

(A.21)

The shift vector is given by

{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}=({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}1},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}1})\;,

(A.22)

where
{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
acts on
({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}})\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}(2)}^{mw}
by translation:

(A.24)

These orbits are the magnetic lattice
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
of the true gauge group
G=\widetilde{G}/\mathrm{U}(1)
.

We can again parametrise
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
in many different ways. We will show a few of these here.

1.

Fix
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}0}
. Let us depict the points in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying the constraint as red dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as red lines:

(A.25)

We can see that every
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbit in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
is represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
. Furthermore, restricting to the shaded part via the constraint
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}\leq{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}
, we get a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}/W_{G}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}(2)/\mathrm{U}(1)}^{mw}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{SU}(2)/\mathbb{Z}_{2}}^{mw}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. Note that fixing
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}=a
for any
a\in\mathbb{Z}
works just as well. Note also that we could instead have imposed this constraint on
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}
instead of
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}
.

2.

Fix
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}\in\{{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0},{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}1}\}
. This is again a more interesting case.

Let us first depict the points in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}={\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}
as orange dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as orange lines:

(A.26)

We can see that not all
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
are represented, just as in the previous example. However, this case is quite different. The
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits indicated in orange make up
\Gamma_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}^{mw}
, and those located in the shaded area represent
\Gamma_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}^{mw}/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
. Since
\mathrm{SU}(2)
is the double cover of
G=\mathrm{SU}(2)/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
, we can see that choosing
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}={\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}
corresponds to picking a different global structure of the true gauge group.

Let us now depict the points in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}={\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}1}
as purple dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as purple lines:

(A.28)

where all
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
are represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
.

Note that fixing
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}\in\{a,b\}
for any
a,b\in\mathbb{Z}
with
a
even and
b
odd works as well. Note further that
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1,2}}=a
for any
a\in\mathbb{Z}
with
a
even picks the magnetic lattice for
\mathrm{SU}(2)
instead of
G=\mathrm{SU}(2)/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
.

(A.34)

These orbits are the magnetic lattice
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
of the true gauge group
G=\widetilde{G}/\mathrm{U}(1)
.

We can parametrise
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
in many different ways. We will show a few of these here

1.

Fix
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}\in\{0,1,2\}
. We depict the points in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
obeying
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}\in\{0,1,2\}
as red dots, and the corresponding
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits as red lines:

(a)

{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}m_{1}}=0
:

(A.37)

Combining the three we see that all
\Lambda_{\color[rgb]{0.2148,0.6641,0.1914}\delta}
-orbits in
\Gamma_{\widetilde{G}}^{mw}
are represented exactly once, and hence we have a good parametrisation of
\Gamma_{G}^{mw}
.

.

Appendix B
Quotients
\mathbb{H}^{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}

In this section we produce quivers which are unframed, simply-laced, loop-free and unitary, with one special unitary node, whose Coulomb branch is the quotient
\mathbb{H}^{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}
.

The quotients
\mathbb{H}^{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}
we study here are specified not only by
n
and
k
, but also by an
n
-tuple of charges
q=(q_{1}\ldots,q_{n})
, where
q_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor\}
. After picking a complex structure
\mathbb{H}^{n}=\mathbb{C}^{2n}
, with
(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})
the coordinates of
\mathbb{C}^{2n}
, a quotient is defined by the action:

\begin{split}\mathbb{Z}_{k}\ni 1:\quad\mathbb{C}^{2n}&\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{2n}\\
x_{i}&\mapsto\omega_{k}^{q_{i}}x_{i}\\
y_{i}&\mapsto\omega_{k}^{-q_{i}}y_{i}~,\quad\textnormal{where }\omega_{k}=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{k}}\end{split}

(B.1)

We can introduce a
\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor
-tuple
\mathfrak{q}=(\mathfrak{q}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{q}_{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor})
where
\mathfrak{q}_{j}
is the number of times
j
appears in
q
. This allows for the following notation of the quotient:

h_{n,k,\mathfrak{q}}=\mathbb{H}^{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}\textnormal{ with charges given by }\mathfrak{q}~,

(B.2)

with the shorthand notation:

h_{n,k}:=h_{n,k,(n,0,\ldots,0)}~.

(B.3)

The Hilbert series of the quotient is computed via the Molien sum:

\mathrm{HS}(h_{n,k,\mathfrak{q}};t)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{s=1}^{k}\prod_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor}\frac{1}{(1-\omega_{k}^{sj}t)^{\mathfrak{q}_{j}}(1-\omega_{k}^{-sj}t)^{\mathfrak{q}_{j}}}~.

(B.4)

The global symmetry
G
of the quotient (as a hyper-Kähler space) is

G=\left\{\begin{matrix}\bigoplus_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor}\mathfrak{u}(\mathfrak{q}_{j})&k\textnormal{ odd}\\
\bigoplus_{j=1}^{\frac{k}{2}-1}\mathfrak{u}(\mathfrak{q}_{j})\oplus\mathfrak{usp}(2\mathfrak{q}_{\frac{k}{2}})&k\textnormal{ even}\end{matrix}\right.~.

(B.5)

2.

Replacing one
\U(k)

\mathrm{SU}(k)
node,
21
21

21

Replacing an
\U(k)
node with an
\mathrm{SU}(k)
is implemented by picking a specific sublattice of the magnetic lattice of the original quiver. One could pick other sublattices to produce different discrete quotients.
the Coulomb branch of the resulting quiver will be a

(B.7)

3.

The resulting Coulomb branch may have a free part, i.e. it is of the form
\mathbb{H}^{d}\times\mathbb{H}^{n-d}/\mathbb{Z}_{k}
. Strap off the free part by replacing the

\U(k)
nodes with a
-1
balance by
\U(k-1)
nodes iteratively, until there are no more unitary nodes of balance
-1
. For example:

(B.11)

Special quivers.

Let us construct some special quivers. We start with an
E_{n}
affine Dynkin quiver, whose Coulomb branch is
\overline{\mathrm{min}.E_{n}}
, and we lower the rank of a single node by
1
. This produces a quiver whose Coulomb branch is freely generated. We can turn one of the unitary nodes in the resulting quiver into a special unitary node, then strap off the free part as explained before. The resulting quiver is either part of the (
B.10
) family, or it is given in Table
2
below.
